</div>
<figcaption markdown="1">**1. Connection and node:** confirm the intended driver. **2. State:** calibration, activation and faults. **3. Command mode:** setpoints and jog controls. **4. Live telemetry:** measured position, speed and current. This screenshot uses **Mock CAN (demo)**, not physical hardware.</figcaption>
</figure>

**Check:** after connecting real hardware, the state and identity belong to your driver. If they do not appear, check the transport, selected port, supply and TX/RX wiring before trying to move.

## Try it without hardware

Open [Motor GUI](https://motorgui.com/), choose **Mock CAN (demo)**, and press **Connect**. The motor and gripper panels run in the browser without a port picker. Motor calibration (`#Cal`) still requires a real UART connection; the CAN demo does not perform it.

## What next

[Calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/05-setup/calibration/) is the first thing to do with a connected driver;
[Working in Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/motor-gui/) covers everyday use: moving the motor, the plots, recordings,
several motors on a bus.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/05-setup/terminal/ -->

# The serial terminal

Motor GUI is the usual way to work with the driver; a plain serial terminal is the alternative, and it is what
the console inside Motor GUI is. Everything in this manual that is done in the GUI is also one `#` command, and
the terminal shows the driver's answers exactly as it prints them, which is useful when something does not work.

The driver talks on its UART connector at 256000 baud, 8N1, 3.3 V. Any terminal that sends a line ending in
CR+LF works.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![The UART connector and the adapter](../assets/UART connection.webp){ width="700" }
  <figcaption>Figure 12: The UART connector. TX of the driver goes to RX of the adapter and RX to TX.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Connecting

1. Plug the [USB-to-serial adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/usb-to-serial-adapter) into the UART
   connector with the [UART cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/uart-cable). With another adapter: 3.3 V
   only, and cross TX and RX: the driver's TX to the adapter's RX, the driver's RX to the adapter's TX.
2. Connect the motor supply. The adapter's 3.3 V powers the driver's logic, so the driver answers over UART with
   only the adapter plugged in, but it reports a Vbus error and refuses calibration and every motion command
   until the 12 to 29 V supply is on.
3. Find the adapter's port: `COM…` on Windows, `/dev/ttyUSB…` or `/dev/ttyACM…` on Linux and macOS.

!!! danger
    5 V on the UART pins destroys the board.

## A terminal

=== "PuTTY"
    PuTTY needs to send CR+LF when you press Enter, which the stock build cannot. Use the
    [modified PuTTY](https://www.grzegorz.net/pliki/putty-crlf.zip): under *Terminal → Keyboard* select the CR LF
    option, then open the serial port at 256000.

    | Keyboard setting | Session |
    |---|---|
    | ![PuTTY keyboard tab](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/PUTTY2.PNG){ width="420" } | ![PuTTY session](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/PUTTY1.PNG){ width="420" } |

=== "VS Code (PlatformIO)"
    With the [firmware project](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-Micro-BLDC-controller/tree/Bootloader_main/Spectral%20BLDC%20Firmware)
    open in VS Code with the PlatformIO extension, the serial monitor (the plug icon in the status bar) uses the
    speed and the `send_on_enter` filter from `platformio.ini`, so a line goes out with CR+LF when you press
    Enter.

    | platformio.ini | The monitor |
    |---|---|
    | ![platformio.ini](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/vscode1.PNG){ width="420" } | ![The serial monitor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/vscode2.PNG){ width="420" } |

=== "Arduino IDE"
    Select the adapter's port under *Tools*, any board (the monitor does not care), open the serial monitor, set
    256000 baud and *Both NL & CR* as the line ending.

    ![Arduino serial monitor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/Arduino3.PNG){ width="420" }

## The first commands

```
#Info
```

prints the driver's identity: the hardware and firmware version, the serial number, the motor parameters and the
calibration state. `#Help` (firmware 106 and newer) prints a short command reference, `#Error` the active errors.

Every command starts with `#`, and a Set/Get command takes one number after a space: `#P 16384` moves to position
16384; `#P` alone prints the position. Names are case-sensitive. The whole set is in the
[UART commands](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/) reference, and [Over UART](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/uart/) explains the
protocol.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/05-setup/calibration/ -->

# Calibration

Calibration teaches the driver its motor: it checks the magnet and the supply, measures the motor's phase
resistance and inductance and computes the current loop gains from them, spins the motor in open loop to find
the pole pairs and the direction, checks the order of the phases and aligns the encoder to the rotor field, and
measures the motor constants Kt, KV and the flux linkage. Nothing about the motor has to be entered first. It
runs once per motor; the result is kept by saving.

!!! danger "The motor turns"
    Calibration spins the motor in both directions, fast at times. Fix the motor to the bench and take everything
    off the shaft.

!!! tip "Supply voltage"
    Calibrate at 24 V. At a lower voltage the resistance, the inductance, KV and Kt come out wrong.

## The settings

The routine uses six settings, which it prints when it starts. The defaults suit motors with a phase resistance
of 2 to 24 Ω; change them only for a motor outside that range.

| Setting | Default | Command | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| Current loop bandwidth | 500 Hz | `#Cbw` | the bandwidth the current loop gains are computed for; too high makes the motor vibrate and whine |
| Resistance voltage | 1000 mV | `#Resv` | the voltage the resistance measurement starts at; it rises until the power reaches the limit below |
| Max power dissipation | 12 W | `#Calpwr` | the power the resistance and inductance measurements may put into the motor |
| Open loop voltage | 5000 mV | `#Openv` | the voltage of the open-loop spin that finds the pole pairs |
| Open loop speed | 20 rad/s | `#Opens` | the electrical speed of that spin |
| Phase search voltage | 5000 mV | `#Vp` | the voltage of the spin that checks the phase order |

!!! danger "Low-resistance motors"
    These voltages are made for motors of 2 Ω and more. On a motor with a much lower resistance, such as a drone
    motor, they drive a destructive current. The Spectral Micro is not made for such motors; if you must try one,
    lower the three voltages and the current limit first.

## 1. Restore the defaults

The EEPROM of a new driver, or of one that ran another motor, can hold values that do not fit: another motor's
parameters, or junk that shows as `-1` in `#Info`. Calibration starts from what is there, so start from the factory
values.

=== "Motor GUI"
    *Default* in the settings.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Default
    ```

This also resets the serial number, hardware version and batch date the driver reports; note what `#Info` printed
if you need them. [Saving the configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/05-setup/saving/) says what else it does.

## 2. Run it

=== "Motor GUI"
    Start the calibration. The driver enters *Calibration mode* and the GUI shows its log step by step; when it
    finishes, the resistance, inductance and pole pairs it measured, the phase order and direction, Kt, KV and the
    flux linkage appear in the settings.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Cal
    ```

The LED flashes every 0.5 s while the routine runs, and the driver prints each step as it goes. The numbers below
are those of one tested motor; yours will differ:

```
----------------
Calibration mode
-----Settings-----
Current loop bandwidth: 500.00Hz
Resistance voltage: 1000mV
Max Power dissipation: 12.00W
Open loop voltage: 5000mV
Open loop Speed: 20.00Rad/s
Phase search voltage: 5000mV
----------------
Magnet test: Passed
Vbus test: Passed
Resistance = 7.026575Ohm
Inductance = 0.001492H
Kp_iq = ...
Ki_iq = ...
Pole pair = 11
Dir = 1
Phase order = 2
Phase order is good!
KV is: ...
Kt is: ...
Flux linkage is: ...
----------------
Calibration success!
Save config with #Save
Going to idle!
----------------
```

What the steps are:

| Step | What happens | Fails with |
|---|---|---|
| Magnet test | the encoder sees enough field: a magnet is there and close enough. The test says nothing about centring, the gap or the glue | `Magnet test: Failed`: magnet missing, too far, or axially magnetised |
| Vbus test | the supply is within limits | `Vbus test: Failed` |
| Resistance | a rising voltage is put on the windings and the current measured; the motor clicks. The resistance follows from the two | `Resistance test: Failed`: no current flows, a phase is not connected, or the motor is far outside the 2 to 24 Ω range |
| Inductance | a voltage step and the rate at which the current rises give the inductance. Kp_iq and Ki_iq are computed from R, L and the bandwidth | `Inductance test: Failed` |
| Open loop | the stator field is turned at the open-loop speed and the encoder watched: the pole pairs are the ratio of electrical to mechanical turns, and the direction the rotor turned is remembered as `Dir` | `Open loop: Failed`: the encoder saw no rotation |
| Phase order | a current command must move the rotor the expected way, and the encoder's zero is aligned to the rotor field (the angle offset, `#Offset`). A motor that does not respond gets a second try at another angle | `Commutation/alignment check failed!`, `Motor did not respond as expected to a current command...` and a line `Spin-confirm delta: … ticks (need > …), Vbus: … mV` that says how far the motor turned and at what voltage |
| Kt, KV, flux linkage | the motor spins fast for a moment and the constants are computed from the back-EMF | — |

!!! note "The measured values are estimates"
    The resistance, the inductance and the motor constants differ a little from one run to the next, and KV, and
    with it Kt and the flux linkage, can be off by a factor of two or three on cheap motors with uneven windings.
    For the loops this does not matter; for a torque estimate in newton-metres, measure Kt yourself.

## 3. Save

=== "Motor GUI"
    **Save**. The GUI marks *Unsaved changes* until you do.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Save
    ```

Without it the calibration is gone at the next power cycle. The driver goes to idle and the LED shows normal
operation; `#Info` shows *Calibrated*, the pole pairs, the resistance and inductance, Kt and KV, the phase order
and the commutation direction.

## When to calibrate again

- After changing the motor, the magnet or the wiring.
- After restoring the defaults.
- After a firmware update that clears the calibration (a release note says so when it does).

A calibration that reports success but a motor that runs badly afterwards usually means the magnet moved on the
shaft between calibration and use: fix the magnet and calibrate again.

## Troubleshooting

| Message | Cause |
|---|---|
| `Magnet test: Failed` | no magnet, magnet too far (more than about 1.5 mm), or an axially magnetised magnet |
| `Vbus test: Failed` | supply off, too low, or the cable the wrong way round (if the driver survived it) |
| `Resistance test: Failed`, `Inductance test: Failed` | a phase not connected or shorted; a motor far outside the 2 to 24 Ω range |
| the motor wobbles left and right and the routine fails | one phase is not connected |
| `Open loop: Failed` | the motor did not turn: a phase open, the open-loop voltage (`#Openv`) too low for a high-resistance motor, the supply's current limit set too low |
| `Commutation/alignment check failed!` | the motor did not respond to the current command: a phase open, a current limit at 0, a magnet that slips. Run `#Cal` again. Firmware 101 printed `Phase order is wrong! Switch motor phases and try again!` here; since 105 the wiring is compensated and swapping wires does not help |
| the routine stops in a step and prints nothing more | reset the driver (`#Reset`) and try again |
| success, but the LED stays on and no error is reported | `#Info` shows `-1` somewhere: the EEPROM is not in the firmware's layout; restore the defaults and calibrate again |
| the resistance, KV or Kt look wrong | the supply was not 24 V, or the motor is one of the uneven ones; see the note above |

Calibration runs over the serial connection only: a terminal, or Motor GUI over the serial adapter, not over CAN.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/05-setup/tuning/ -->

# Current limit and loop tuning

Calibration leaves the driver with current loop gains computed for your motor and with conservative velocity and
position gains. Two things remain: the current limit, which you must set for your motor, and the loop gains, which
you tune if the defaults do not suit it. Motor GUI shows the motor's response on its plots while you change a gain,
which is what makes tuning quick.

## The current limit

Set the current limit to the rated phase current of your motor in mA. The firmware's default of 1000 mA suits the
gimbal motors in [Tested motors](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/03-technical-data/tested-motors/); a motor rated for more can go up to the
driver's 2800 mA. The firmware clamps the limit to the
driver's 2800 mA and does not trip on phase current by itself; the MOSFET driver's hardware protection only
catches a hard fault. A limit above the motor's rating overheats the motor.

=== "Motor GUI"
    In the limits set the current limit, then **Save**.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Ilim 1500
    #Save
    ```

Crunching and whining sounds at speed usually mean the current limit, or the current loop gains, are too high.

## The loops

<figure markdown="span">
  ![The cascaded loops](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/cascadeloop.webp){ width="800" }
  <figcaption>Figure 13: The position loop commands the velocity loop, which commands the current loop.</figcaption>
</figure>

Tune from the inside out: the current loop first, then velocity, then position. Before you start:

- The motor must be calibrated and without active errors; the driver refuses the control modes otherwise.
- Fix the motor to the bench, nothing on the shaft. A loop that oscillates can shake a loose motor off the table.
- If the defaults oscillate, lower all gains until the motor is quiet, then raise them one at a time in small steps.

=== "Motor GUI"
    The gains are in the settings: change one, *Apply gains*, command a move with the jog controls and read the
    response on the plots. *Apply preset* loads a starting set for a kind of motor. **Save** when you are done.

=== "Terminal"
    Each gain is a command: `#Kpiq 0.5`, `#Kpv 0.02`, …, then `#Save`. Command a move with `#Iq`, `#V` or `#P`
    and judge the response by ear and by `#Cyc 20`, which streams position, speed and current.

### The current loop

The current loop is a PI controller that turns a current request into a voltage. Calibration sets its gains
`Kpiq` and `Kiiq` from the motor's resistance and inductance and the bandwidth (`#Cbw`, 500 Hz by default; set it
before calibrating). These computed gains suit most gimbal motors; tune by hand if the motor hums or responds slowly:

1. Raise `Kpiq` until the motor starts to hum or oscillate, then back off 20 %.
2. Raise `Kiiq` the same way, then back off a little.
3. Test with a current setpoint of a few hundred mA (*Jog current*, or `#Iq 300`): the motor should push with a
   steady, quiet torque. Keep the current well under the limit.

A higher bandwidth responds faster to a disturbance and is louder; 800 Hz and more is common in industry, and
useful for legged robots.

### The velocity loop

1. Raise `Kpv` until the motor oscillates at a steady speed command, then back off 20 %.
2. Raise `Kiv` slowly until it oscillates, then back off a little. `Kiv` is an integrator: too much makes the
   motor unstable, none leaves a steady-state error.
3. Test with a speed setpoint (*Jog velocity*, or `#V 20000`; 16384 ticks per second is one revolution per
   second) and with different speeds.

### The position loop

1. Raise `Kpp` until the motor overshoots or oscillates when it reaches a target, then back off.
2. Test with a position step (*Jog position*, or `#P 16384` and `#P 0`): one revolution and back. The response
   should be quick, without overshoot; the plot shows both.

### Testing

Run the motor over the whole range of speeds and loads it will see, with a load if you can, and adjust. Then save.

## Impedance (PD) mode

<figure markdown="span">
  ![The PD loop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/PDloop.webp){ width="800" }
  <figcaption>Figure 14: The impedance loop: a spring (KP) and a damper (KD) around the position setpoint, plus a current feedforward.</figcaption>
</figure>

In PD mode the motor behaves like a spring and a damper: the torque is `KP × (setpoint − position) + KD × (speed
setpoint − speed) + feedforward current`. Set `KP` and `KD` (the gains, or `#KP`, `#KD`, or Send_PD_Gains), then
command with `#PD`, `#PDV` and `#PDI` or Send_data_pack_PD. Start with a small `KP` and `KD` of 0, raise `KP` until
the motor holds position firmly, then add `KD` until it stops ringing. The [theory corner](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/appendix/theory/)
explains the loop.

## Limits

- The velocity limit (`#Vlimit`) clamps the speed the loops may command, in encoder ticks per second. A rough
  maximum for your motor is 0.8 × Vbus × KV × 16384 / 60 ticks per second, with KV from calibration.
- The voltage limit (`#Vlim`) clamps the voltage of the current loops in mV; 0 uses the supply voltage.
- `#Rstint 1` resets the integrators on every new setpoint, which avoids windup when a program sends one setpoint
  after another with large steps.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/05-setup/saving/ -->

# Saving the configuration

Nothing you set survives a power cycle until you save it.

=== "Motor GUI"
    **Save**. The GUI marks *Unsaved changes* until you do.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Save
    ```

Saving writes the whole configuration to the EEPROM: the motor parameters and the calibration, every gain and
limit, the CAN node ID, the heartbeat and watchdog settings, the thermistor and LED settings and the gripper flag.
Over CAN, Send_Save_config does the same. Save after calibration, after tuning, and after changing the node ID.

## The defaults

=== "Motor GUI"
    *Default* in the settings.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Default
    ```

Restoring the defaults writes the factory values to the EEPROM and reloads them. It also resets the serial
number, the hardware version and the batch date the driver reports, and clears the gripper flag, the heartbeat
rate and the watchdog; note what the driver reports before you use it. The defaults are listed in the
[Defaults](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/defaults/) reference.

Use it before the first calibration of a motor, after a firmware update when the driver behaves oddly, and when
the state shows nonsense values (a `-1`
where a number should be): the EEPROM then holds a layout the firmware does not expect.

## What the driver reports

The state Motor GUI shows, and `#Info` prints, is what is in the EEPROM and what the driver measures: hardware
and firmware version, serial number, calibration state, resistance, inductance, pole pairs, Kt and KV, the gains
and limits, the CAN ID, and the active errors. It is the first thing to look at when something is off, and the
thing to copy into a bug report.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/ -->

# Operation

How a calibrated driver is used: the control modes and what each one does, the two ways to talk to the driver and
the two tools on top of them, what happens when something goes wrong, and gripper mode.

## In this chapter

- [Control modes](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/modes/)
- [Over UART](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/uart/)
- [Over CAN](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/can/)
- [With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/python/)
- [Working in Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/motor-gui/)
- [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/errors/)
- [Gripper mode](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/gripper-mode/)

The exact layout of every message and command is in the [API reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/modes/ -->

# Control modes

The driver is always in one control mode. A command that carries a setpoint switches to the mode that uses it;
`#Idle` or Send_Idle switches back to idle. The driver refuses the closed-loop modes while it is not calibrated or
while an error is active.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> NotCalibrated: power-up, no saved calibration
    [*] --> Idle: power-up, saved calibration
    NotCalibrated --> Calibration: #Cal
    Calibration --> Idle: success, #Save
    Calibration --> NotCalibrated: a test fails
    Idle --> ControlMode: a setpoint
    ControlMode --> Idle: #Idle, Send_Idle
    ControlMode --> Error: a fault
    Idle --> Error: a fault
    Error --> Idle: #Clear, cause gone
```

A setpoint is `#P`, `#V`, `#Iq`, `#PD` or a CAN motion frame, and a new setpoint switches the mode without
passing through idle; a fault is any of the errors on [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/errors/).

| ControlMode | What the motor does | Entered by | Setpoint unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Idle | nothing: coasts (phases open) or brakes (phases shorted), as set by `#Brake` or Send_Settings | `#Idle`, Send_Idle, `#Clear`, errors | — |
| Position | holds and moves to a position with the cascade of position, velocity and current loops | `#P`, Send_data_pack_1 (8 bytes) | encoder ticks |
| Velocity | turns at a speed with the velocity and current loops | `#V`, Send_data_pack_1 (5 bytes) | encoder ticks/s |
| Current (torque) | applies a current, so a torque, with the current loop alone | `#Iq`, Send_data_pack_1 (2 bytes) | mA |
| PD (impedance) | behaves like a spring and a damper around a position, with `KP` and `KD` | `#PD`, Send_data_pack_PD | encoder ticks |
| Voltage torque | applies a voltage on the q axis directly, without the current loop | `#Uq` | mV |
| Open loop | turns the stator field at a set electrical speed without the encoder in the loop; the rotor follows it like a stepper | `#Openloop` | electrical speed |
| Gripper | runs the gripper state machine: move to a jaw position with a speed and a current limit | `#Grippos`, Send_gripper_data_pack (with `#Gripper 1`) | 0 to 255 |
| Calibration | the calibration routine, or the gripper calibration | `#Cal`, `#Gripcal` | — |

## Units

- **Position** is in encoder ticks: 16384 per revolution of the motor shaft, counting up without limit over
  several revolutions. Positive is counter-clockwise seen from the encoder side of the board, see below.
- **Speed** is in encoder ticks per second: 16384 is one revolution per second, 60 rpm.
- **Current** is in mA. Torque is current times the motor's Kt, which calibration finds.
- **Feedforward**: the 8-byte motion frame carries a speed and a current feedforward beside the position, the
  5-byte one a current feedforward beside the speed. They are added after the loops, so a host that knows the
  trajectory can command it directly and leave the loops to correct the rest. Send 0 when you do not use them.

## Try it

<div class="calc" data-ticks-per-rev="16384" data-max-electrical-hz="500" markdown="0">
  <div class="calc__row calc__row--inline">
    <label for="uc-ticks">Ticks (a position, or a speed per second)</label>
    <input id="uc-ticks" type="number" name="ticks" step="1" value="16384">
    <label for="uc-pp">Pole pairs</label>
    <select id="uc-pp" name="pp">
      <option value="7">7</option>
      <option value="11" selected>11 (the gimbal motors)</option>
      <option value="14">14</option>
      <option value="21">21</option>
    </select>
  </div>
  <p class="calc__result">As a position: <strong data-out="turns">1.000</strong> turns, <strong data-out="deg">360.0°</strong> · as a speed: <strong data-out="rpm">60</strong> rpm · the practical maximum for <span data-out="ppout">11</span> pole pairs is about <strong data-out="maxrpm">2727</strong> rpm</p>
  <div class="calc__row calc__row--inline">
    <label for="uc-kt">Kt in Nm/A (what #Kt prints)</label>
    <input id="uc-kt" type="number" name="kt" step="0.01" min="0" value="0.30">
    <label for="uc-ma">Current in mA</label>
    <input id="uc-ma" type="number" name="ma" step="10" value="1000">
  </div>
  <p class="calc__result">Torque: <strong data-out="nm">0.30 Nm</strong>, <strong data-out="ncm">30 N·cm</strong></p>
</div>

The units of this page, with your numbers: 16384 encoder ticks per turn, the practical speed limit from the
electrical frequency the control loop can follow ([Ratings and limits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/03-technical-data/ratings/)), and
the torque as Kt times the current.

## Positive rotation

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Positive rotation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/Positive_rotation.webp){ width="520" }
  <figcaption>Figure 15: Looking at the encoder side of the board, the side that faces the magnet, positive rotation is counter-clockwise. A positive current turns the motor that way, a positive speed too, and the position grows.</figcaption>
</figure>

The direction is tied to the encoder, not to the wiring: since firmware 105 calibration compensates the order of
the phases, so the motor turns the same way whichever wire went to which terminal.

## Which mode am I in?

`#Mode` prints the mode: `Idle mode`, `Position control`, `Speed control`, `Current control`, `PD control`,
`Open loop`, `Gripper mode` or `Gripper calib mode`. The voltage-torque mode has no label of its own in this
release; `#Info` and the behaviour of the motor are the check there.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/uart/ -->

# Over UART

The serial port is the interactive way to use the driver: you type a command, the driver answers in text. It is
the only way to calibrate, and the quickest way to try a setting. For real-time control of several motors use CAN.

## The protocol

A command is `#`, a name, optionally a space and one number, and a line ending:

```
#P 16384
#P
#Cal
```

- The name is case-sensitive and matches the firmware's spelling exactly (`#Kpiq`, not `#kpiq`); at most 19
  characters, the number at most 19 characters, both together at most 20.
- The line ends with LF (`\n`); a CR before it is accepted. Terminals send CR+LF when you press Enter, with the
  setting described in [The serial terminal](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/05-setup/terminal/).
- A **Set/Get** command with a number sets the value and prints it; without a number it only prints it. `#P 16384`
  moves to position 16384 and prints the position; `#P` prints the position.
- An **action** command takes no number: `#Cal`, `#Save`, `#Idle`.
- A command the parser does not know is answered with `Unknown command`. A few names the parser
  accepts have no handler and are answered with nothing; the [UART reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/) lists them.
- 256000 baud, 8N1, 3.3 V.

## The driver only answers

The driver never sends anything on its own, except with the cyclic commands: `#Cyc 100` makes it print position,
speed and Iq every 100 ms as `$ <position> <speed> <Iq>` (for BetterSerialPlotter), `#Cyca 100` as
`Position:x,Speed:y,Iq:z` (for the Arduino plotter); `#Cyc` or `#Cyca` without a number stops it.

## Typical sessions

A first test after calibration:

```
#Ilim 1500        current limit for the motor
#V 16384          one revolution per second
#V 0
#P 0              back to the start
#Idle
```

Tuning:

```
#Kpv 0.02
#Kiv 0.001
#V 30000
#Save
```

Status:

```
#Info
#Error
#Temp
#Vbus
```

Every command is in the [UART reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/), grouped by what it does.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/can/ -->

# Over CAN

CAN is the interface for running a machine: compact frames, a fixed cost per message, up to 16 drivers on one bus,
and a host that can be a PC, a microcontroller or a robot control box. The driver answers a motion command with
its position, speed and current in the same frame exchange, so a control loop on the host needs one frame out and
one frame back per motor and cycle.

## The frame

CAN 2.0 data frames with 11-bit identifiers at 1 Mbit/s. The identifier carries the node, the command and the
error state:

<figure markdown="span">
  ![The CAN identifier](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/CANID.PNG){ width="600" }
  <figcaption>Figure 16: Bits 10 to 7 of the identifier are the node ID, bits 6 to 1 the command ID, bit 0 the error bit.</figcaption>
</figure>

- **Node ID**, bits 10 to 7: which driver, 0 to 15. A driver acts only on frames with its own node ID and sends
  with it. Set it with `#CANID` or Send_CAN_ID and save; every driver ships as node 0. Use 0 to 13: the
  [bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/07-firmware/the-bootloader/) reserves 14 and 15, and a driver on one of those cannot be
  updated over CAN.
- **Command ID**, bits 6 to 1: which message, 0 to 63. The [CAN reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/) lists all of
  them.
- **Error bit**, bit 0: in a frame from the driver, 1 while any error is active. In a frame from the host it is
  ignored.

So a host sends Send_data_pack_1 (command 2) to node 3 with the identifier `(3 << 7) | (2 << 1)` = 0x184, and the
driver answers with command 3 under `(3 << 7) | (3 << 1) | error`. A lower node ID wins the bus arbitration.

Multi-byte values are big-endian: the most significant byte is in data[0] and goes first. Floats are IEEE 754
single precision. Flags inside a byte are numbered from the most significant bit.

## Three kinds of message

- **Send_…**: the host sends data. Some of these are answered (a motion command with Respond_data_pack_1, the
  gripper command with Respond_Gripper_data_pack); most are not.
- **Send_Respond_…**: the host asks for data with a **remote frame** (the RTR bit set, no data) carrying the
  command ID; the driver answers with a data frame with the same command ID.
- **Respond_…**: frames only the driver sends: the answers above, and the heartbeat.

## A control loop

Send Send_data_pack_1 at a fixed rate, 100 Hz to 1 kHz, with the setpoint for this cycle; read Respond_data_pack_1
for the position, speed and current of the last cycle. Every valid frame resets the watchdog, so with
Send_Watchdog set to a few cycle times the motor stops when the host stops. The heartbeat is the other way round:
Send_Heartbeat_Setup makes the driver send a frame on its own every N ms when it has nothing else to send, so the
host can see it is alive.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Host
    participant D as Driver
    H->>D: Send_Clear_Error
    H->>D: Send_Watchdog: a few cycle times
    H->>D: Send_Heartbeat_Setup: every N ms
    loop every cycle, 100 Hz to 1 kHz
        H->>D: Send_data_pack_1: the setpoint, with the feedforwards
        D-->>H: Respond_data_pack_1: position, speed, current, the error bit
    end
    D-->>H: heartbeat, whenever nothing else was sent for N ms
    Note over D: no valid frame within the watchdog time: watchdog error, the motor stops
```

## From a PC

The [CANvas adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/canvas-usb-to-can-adapter) shows up as a serial port and
speaks slcan; `python-can` opens it with `bustype='slcan'`. The Python library wraps the whole protocol, see
[With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/python/). Any CAN adapter that `python-can` supports works the same way.

## Several drivers

Give each driver its own node ID before you put them on one bus (a bus with two node 0s cannot tell them apart):
connect one driver at a time over UART, `#CANID 3`, `#Save`. Terminate the first and the last node, and wire the
daisy chain as in [Power and the CAN daisy chain](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/04-mounting/power-and-can/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/python/ -->

# With Python

The `Spectral-BLDC` library wraps the CAN protocol: one method per message, and the driver's answers unpacked into
attributes. It runs on Windows, Linux and macOS with any adapter `python-can` supports, such as the CANvas adapter
over slcan.

## Installing

```
pip install Spectral-BLDC
```

The source and the examples are in [Spectral-BLDC-Python](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-Python).
For joints with a gear ratio and an offset, the [Source Robotics Toolbox](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Source-Robotics-Toolbox)
(`pip install SourceRoboticsToolbox`) turns encoder ticks into joint angles.

## The first program

```python
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
import time

# the adapter: a CANvas on COM41 (Windows) or /dev/ttyACM0 (Linux), 1 Mbit/s
comms = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM41', bitrate=1000000)
# the driver with node ID 0
motor = Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=comms)

motor.Send_Clear_Error()

# A configured, calibrated motor with a clear shaft: command one turn for five seconds.
# Each command requests a fresh position/speed/current reply; heartbeat is not required.
try:
    deadline = time.monotonic() + 5.0
    next_cycle = time.monotonic()
    while time.monotonic() < deadline:
        motor.Send_data_pack_1(Position=16384, Speed=0, Current=0)
        reply_deadline = min(deadline, time.monotonic() + 0.02)
        while time.monotonic() < reply_deadline:
            message, ids = comms.receive_can_messages(
                timeout=max(0.0, reply_deadline - time.monotonic()))
            if message is None:
                print("No motion feedback in this cycle; check the bus and node ID")
                break
            if ids.node_id != 0 or ids.command_id != 3:  # Respond_data_pack_1
                continue
            motor.UnpackData(message, ids)
            print(motor.position, motor.speed, motor.current, ids.error_bit)
            if ids.error_bit:
                raise RuntimeError("Driver fault: inspect State_of_Errors before retrying")
            break
        next_cycle += 0.02
        time.sleep(max(0.0, next_cycle - time.monotonic()))
finally:
    motor.Send_Idle()                    # also on Ctrl-C; the shaft no longer holds torque
```

`receive_can_messages` returns the raw `python-can` message and a tuple with the node ID, the command ID and the
error bit of the identifier; `UnpackData` decodes the message into the attributes the message carries. This example resends the same
setpoint at 50 Hz for five seconds, prints only matching motion feedback, and puts the motor in idle when it
ends. Idle releases torque: support any attached mechanism before running it. A missing reply is reported
without claiming that a move finished. Configure and calibrate the driver first ([Quick start](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/quick-start/)).

## What is where

| Library call | Message | What you get back |
|---|---|---|
| `Send_data_pack_1(Position, Speed, Current)` | Send_data_pack_1 | `position`, `speed`, `current` |
| `Send_data_pack_PD(...)` | Send_data_pack_PD | `position`, `speed`, `current` |
| `Send_Respond_Encoder_data()` | Send_Respond_Encoder_data | `position`, `speed` (32-bit) |
| `Send_Respond_State_of_Errors()` | Send_Respond_State_of_Errors | the error attributes |
| `Send_gripper_data_pack(...)` | Send_gripper_data_pack | `gripper_position`, `gripper_current`, the gripper state bits |
| `Send_Limits(...)`, `Send_Velocity_Gains(...)`, ... | the setting messages | nothing; `Send_Save_config()` keeps them |

The complete map of calls to messages is in the [Python library](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/python/) reference, and each
message's bytes in the [CAN reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/).

## Several motors

One `CanCommunication` per bus, one `SpectralCAN` per driver with its node ID. Send to each, then read the bus:
every answer carries the node ID in `ids.node_id`, so route it to the right object.

```python
motors = [Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=i, communication=comms) for i in range(3)]
for m in motors:
    m.Send_Respond_Encoder_data()
for _ in motors:
    message, ids = comms.receive_can_messages(timeout=0.1)
    if message is not None:
        motors[ids.node_id].UnpackData(message, ids)
```

The [Guides](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/guides/) build on this: a quadruped leg, gravity compensation, bilateral teleoperation.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/motor-gui/ -->

# Working in Motor GUI

Everyday use of the driver from [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/05-setup/motor-gui/): moving the motor, watching it, recording
what it does, running several motors, and the few things that only work from the console.

## Moving the motor

The jog controls send setpoints in the matching control mode: *Jog velocity* turns the motor at a speed in encoder
ticks per second (16384 is one revolution per second), *Jog position* moves it to a position in ticks, *Jog
current* applies a torque in mA. *Send setpoint* sends a value in the mode the driver is in. Idle stops the
motor; [Control modes](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/modes/) says what each mode does. With *Live stream while dragging* the setpoint follows
the slider, which is the quickest way to feel a tuning change.

## Watching it

The plots show position, speed and current as the driver reports them. Pan and zoom to a move; hover for the
value. A step in the position setpoint shows overshoot and settling at once, a speed step shows the velocity
loop's response; [Current limit and loop tuning](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/05-setup/tuning/) uses them step by step.

## Recording

A recording keeps the telemetry stream to a file: *New recording*, run the move, *Stop recording*. Record the
response before and after a tuning change to compare them, or a failure to attach to a bug report
([Report a problem](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/support/report-a-problem/)).

## Clearing errors

The errors the driver reports are listed with the state; **Clear errors** sends what `#Clear` does. An error whose
cause is still present comes straight back; [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/errors/) says what each one needs.

## Several motors

Over the CANvas adapter the GUI sees every driver on the bus and addresses each by its node ID. Give each driver
its own ID over the serial adapter first (the CAN node ID in the settings, then Save), terminate the first and the
last node, and set a watchdog (*Watchdog ms*) on a bus that drives something that must not run away:
[Power and the CAN daisy chain](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/04-mounting/power-and-can/), [Over CAN](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/can/).

## Gripper

A driver in gripper mode shows the gripper controls: calibrate the jaws, a position from open to closed, a speed,
a current limit, and the state the gripper reports. *No gripper connection* means the driver is not in gripper
mode or not on the bus. [Gripper mode](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/gripper-mode/).

## Firmware updates

*Firmware update* lists the releases from GitHub and flashes one through the bootloader; on a bus, *Scan
bootloaders* finds the boards. [Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/07-firmware/update/).

## The console

Anything the GUI has no control for is one `#` command away in the console, with the driver's answer below it;
the whole set is in the [UART commands](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/) reference. The cyclic output (`#Cyc`) is what
the GUI's telemetry stream uses over serial, so do not start it by hand while the plots run.

## Reading a fault

<figure class="gui-shot" markdown="1">
<div class="gui-shot__image" markdown="1">

![Motor GUI demo with a latched E-stop fault and the Errors tab open](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/motor-gui/errors-demo.jpg){ width="1000" }

<span class="gui-shot__mark" style="left:1%;top:14%" aria-hidden="true">1</span>
<span class="gui-shot__mark" style="left:7%;top:57%" aria-hidden="true">2</span>
<span class="gui-shot__mark" style="left:13%;top:81%" aria-hidden="true">3</span>
<span class="gui-shot__mark" style="left:7%;top:26%" aria-hidden="true">4</span>

</div>
<figcaption markdown="1">**1. Errors state:** a fault is active. **2. Errors tab:** inspect individual flags. **3. E-stop error:** 1 identifies the latched fault in this simulation. **4. Clear errors:** clear it after removing its cause; a persistent cause returns on the next update. Screenshot captured from **Mock CAN (demo)**.</figcaption>
</figure>

**Check:** after recovery the fault flag returns to 0 and the state shows No errors. If it returns, stop and follow [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/errors/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/errors/ -->

# Errors and recovery

When the driver detects a fault it stops the motor, goes to idle, turns the status LED on steadily and sets the
error bit in every CAN frame it sends. It stays there until the error is cleared.

## Seeing the error

- **The LED**: on and not flashing means error mode (or not calibrated). Three short flashes and a pause is
  normal operation; flashing every 0.5 s is calibration.
- **`#Error`** prints `In error state!` or `No errors!`, followed by one line per active error.
- **Send_Respond_State_of_Errors** returns every flag as a bit; **the error bit** of any frame says whether there
  is one.

| Normal operation | Calibration | Error mode |
|---|---|---|
| ![Three short flashes and a pause](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/Normal.webp){ width="180" } | ![Flashing every 0.5 s](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/Calib.webp){ width="180" } | ![On, steady](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/Error2.webp){ width="180" } |

In error mode the LED does not flash: it stays on, as in the photo on the right.

## The errors

| Error | `#Error` line | Cause | What to do |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vbus | `Vbus error` | the supply voltage is below 9 V or above 29.5 V (`#Vmax`) | check the supply and the cable; a decelerating motor can push the voltage up |
| Encoder | `Encoder error` | the magnet is not detected or the reading is invalid | magnet distance and type, see [The encoder magnet](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/04-mounting/magnet/) |
| Driver | `Driver error (undervoltage, thermal shutdown, or overcurrent)` | the MOSFET driver's own protection tripped | lower the current limit, cool the driver, check for a short between the motor leads |
| Velocity | `Velocity error` | the speed exceeded the limit | lower the commanded speed or raise `#Vlimit` |
| Temperature | `Temp error` | the thermistor reads more than `#Tlim` (75 °C by default), with `#Term 1` | let the motor cool; lower the current limit |
| E-stop | `Received ESTOP command` | Send_ESTOP was received | clear it when it is safe |
| Watchdog | `Watchdog error` | no valid CAN frame within the watchdog time (Send_Watchdog) | the host stopped sending; fix the host, then clear |
| Not calibrated | `Not calibrated` | the motor has not been calibrated since `#Default`, or the EEPROM is invalid | run `#Cal` and `#Save` |
| Current | `Current error` | reserved; this firmware never raises it | — |

## Clearing

`#Clear` or Send_Clear_Error clears the flags and goes to idle. An error whose cause is still present comes
straight back: a Vbus error at 2 V stays until the supply is right; once the supply is 24 V, one `#Clear` returns
the driver to normal operation. The calibration error clears only by calibrating (or, for a motor you know is
calibrated, `#Calibrated 1`).

## When the driver does not answer

- No LED at all: no power. Check DC+ and DC− and the cable orientation.
- LED on, no answer on UART: the baud rate (256000), TX and RX crossed, the adapter's port.
- No answer on CAN: the node ID, the termination (about 60 Ω across the bus, unpowered), 1 Mbit/s on the adapter.
- `#Info` shows `-1` or nonsense: the EEPROM holds a layout the firmware does not expect; `#Default`, then
  calibrate again.

[Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/08-troubleshooting/) goes through the symptoms one by one.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/gripper-mode/ -->

# Gripper mode

A driver can run a gripper instead of a joint: the same board, with a state machine that moves a jaw to a
position between open and closed, at a speed, with a current limit that becomes the grip force, and that reports
when it holds something. The [SSG-48 gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/) is built on the Spectral Micro this way.

## Turning it on

```
#Gripper 1
#Save
```

`#Default` clears the flag again. A driver in gripper mode still answers every other command; the gripper
commands only work with the flag set.

## Calibrating the gripper

After every power-up the gripper has to find its end stops: `#Gripcal` or Send_gripper_calibrate. The jaws move
to both ends; the positions become 0 (open) and 255 (closed). The motor itself must be calibrated (`#Cal`) and
saved before that, once.

## Moving

Over UART:

```
#Gripvel 100       speed, 0 to 255
#Gripcur 400       current limit of the move in mA, the grip force
#Grippos 200       go to position 200 (0 open, 255 closed); also activates the gripper
```

Over CAN, Send_gripper_data_pack carries position, speed and current in one frame with the activate and action
bits; the driver answers with Respond_Gripper_data_pack: the position, the measured current, whether it is moving,
and the object detection:

| Object detection | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | moving |
| 1 | an object was detected while closing: the jaws stopped on it and hold it with the current limit |
| 2 | an object was detected while opening |
| 3 | the position was reached |

An empty Send_gripper_data_pack (0 bytes) only asks for the state. Send_gripper_data_pack's E-stop bit raises the
gripper E-stop error; `#Gripstop 1` does the same over UART.

!!! warning "Current"
    The firmware does not limit the current you give a gripper move. The safe range depends on the gripper's mechanics and motor; the
    [SSG-48 manual](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/) gives it for that gripper. The driver's hard limit is 2800 mA.

## Where the details are

The bytes of the two gripper frames are in the [CAN reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/gripper/), the UART commands in
the [UART reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/gripper/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/07-firmware/ -->

# Firmware

The driver's firmware is open source and released as numbered builds. A driver shipped with firmware 105 or newer carries a bootloader and updates itself over UART or CAN; an older driver needs the bootloader installed once with
a programming adapter.

## In this chapter

- [Releases and versions](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/07-firmware/releases/): how releases are numbered, how to see which one a driver runs, what the
  release notes contain
- [The bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/07-firmware/the-bootloader/): what it is, how the driver boots, how it is entered, its protocol and tools
- [Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/07-firmware/update/): the normal update, with Motor GUI, the bootloader's command-line
  tool, or a PAR6 control box
- [Installing the bootloader on an older board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/07-firmware/bootloader/): for a driver that runs firmware 104 or older
- [Building from source](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/07-firmware/building/): PlatformIO, the memory layout, uploading with a programming adapter

The release notes of every release up to the one this site describes are in the appendix,
[Firmware release notes](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/appendix/firmware-release-notes/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/07-firmware/releases/ -->

# Releases and versions

A firmware release is a number: 101, 104, 105, … Every release is a tag `V<number>` in the
[firmware repository](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-Micro-BLDC-controller) and a GitHub release that
carries the image `spectral-bldc-firmware-V<number>.bin`, a manifest `firmware.json` with the image's size, SHA-256 and
the commit it was built from, and the release notes. The notes are the firmware's changelog; the
[appendix](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/appendix/firmware-release-notes/) collects them.

## Which release does my driver run?

```
#Info
```

prints `Software version: <number>` among the rest. Over CAN, Send_Respond_Device_Info returns it as the third
byte. From firmware 105 the number is the build's own version; before that it was read from the EEPROM and could
be stale after an update until `#Default`.

## Which release does this site describe?

The one in the version box on the [landing page](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/) and in the version selector in the header. When a
newer release changes what a page says, a new version of the site is published and the previous one stays
reachable from the selector. The [compatibility table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/appendix/compatibility/) says which releases go with
which bootloader, Python library and PAR6 runtime.

## The STEPFOC counterpart

Each Spectral Micro release has a [STEPFOC](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/) release with the same
changes; the numbers differ by one (Spectral Micro 107 is STEPFOC 108). The compatibility table lists the pairs.

## The two branches

Releases from 105 on are built from the `Bootloader_main` branch of the repository, whose firmware is linked
to run above the bootloader. The `main` branch holds the firmware of release 104 and earlier, linked to run without a bootloader, and is not
updated. A board running 101 or 104 is documented by version `101` of this site (104 differs from 101 only by the
Send_Voltage_Limit message); to move it to a current release, see [Installing the bootloader on an older board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/07-firmware/bootloader/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/07-firmware/the-bootloader/ -->

# The bootloader

Every driver shipped with firmware 105 or newer carries a small bootloader in the first 12 KB of its flash. It
starts the firmware on a normal boot, and it loads a new firmware over UART or CAN when a host asks, so a driver is
updated without a programming adapter and without opening anything. The bootloader is open source:
[stm32f103c-bootloader](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/stm32f103c-bootloader), shared with STEPFOC.

## Memory layout

| Address | Contents |
|---|---|
| `0x08000000` – `0x080022FF` | the bootloader (about 9 KB) |
| `0x08002C00` – `0x08002FFF` | the bootloader's configuration page: the board ID, the firmware's page count and CRC, the bootloader's build version |
| `0x08003000` – `0x0801FFFF` | the firmware (up to 116 KB) |
| RAM `0x20001000` | a magic word the bootloader sets to hand over to the firmware |

The firmware is linked to start at `0x08003000` and sets its vector table there (`VECT_TAB_OFFSET=0x3000`); the
first `0x3000` bytes belong to the bootloader and the firmware never touches them.

## What happens at boot

1. On a reset, the bootloader runs first. If the magic word is in RAM and the reset was a software reset, it
   checks the firmware's stack pointer and reset vector and jumps straight into the firmware: about 10 ms, the
   normal boot.
2. Otherwise it initialises the clocks, CAN, UART and its watchdog, and **listens for a host for 2 s**.
3. With no host, and a firmware whose stored CRC is valid, it sets the magic word and resets; the next boot takes
   the fast path.
4. With a host talking, it stays as long as the host keeps talking: 3 s after the last command, 60 s once a flash
   is in progress. Any `PING` resets the timer.
5. With no valid firmware (never flashed, or a flash that was interrupted), it stays in bootloader mode and waits.
   The LED is off; the driver answers nothing on `#Info`.

## Entering the bootloader

- **From the firmware**: `#Reset` over UART or Send_Reset (command 14) over CAN. Since firmware 105 both reset
  the driver into the bootloader's 2 s window; the host tools send them for you.
- **At power-on**: the 2 s window after every power-up, if the host is already polling.
- **Always**, when there is no valid firmware.

## The board ID

The bootloader has a board ID of its own, 0 to 13, stored in its configuration page. 14 and 15 do not exist
for it: its command frame, identifier `0x700`, decodes as node 14 in the firmware's identifier scheme, so those
two node IDs are reserved. **Give drivers node IDs 0 to 13.** The firmware accepts `#CANID 14` and `15`, but the
bootloader then keeps its old board ID and a firmware update over CAN cannot reach the driver. The firmware keeps it in step with its CAN node ID: setting the node ID (`#CANID`,
Send_CAN_ID) writes the bootloader's board ID too, so a driver answers the host tools under its node ID. A
replacement board ships as ID 0; two boards with the same ID on one bus corrupt each other's flash stream, so
give the new board its ID alone on the bus first (`set-id` in the host tool).

## Transports and protocol

Over **CAN** (1 Mbit/s, standard 11-bit identifiers) the host commands on identifier `0x700` with 8 data bytes
(`board_id`, `cmd`, two parameters); the board replies on `0x701 + board_id` with 5 bytes (`board_id`, `cmd`,
error code, a 16-bit parameter); the firmware image streams in bulk frames on `(board_id << 7) | sequence`,
16 frames of 8 bytes per chunk, with no reply per frame. Over **UART** (256000 baud) the same commands travel in
framed packets `[0xBB][CMD][LEN][BOARD_ID][DATA…][CRC16]` with the same 5-byte reply.

Commands: `WBUF` (1), `WPAGE` (2), `WCRC` (3), `PING` (4), `SET_ID` (5), `ERASE_APP` (6), `STREAM_BEGIN` (7),
`STREAM_STATUS` (8). Error codes: `0` OK, `1` invalid offset, `2` invalid CRC, `3` flash write failed, `4` invalid
page number. A flash is: ping, reset the firmware if it answers, ping until the bootloader answers, `ERASE_APP`
(about 3.5 s), then for each 1 KB page `STREAM_BEGIN`, 8 chunks of 16 frames, `STREAM_STATUS`, `WPAGE` with the
page's CRC32; finally `WCRC` with the page count and the image's CRC32. The bootloader stores the CRC and
reboots into the new firmware. The full wire protocol is in the bootloader repository's `docs/PROTOCOL.md`.

## The host side

| Tool | Transport | Use |
|---|---|---|
| [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/05-setup/motor-gui/) | serial adapter (Web Serial) or CANvas | one driver on the bench, releases fetched from GitHub |
| `host_tools/bl_flash.py` in the bootloader repository | slcan or gs_usb CAN adapters, or UART | scripts, several boards, `list`, `set-id`, `flash --erase-first` |
| the PAR6 control box's `flash_motor_firmware.py` and the dashboard's Firmware tab | the robot's own CAN bus | every joint of a robot, from the box |

[Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/07-firmware/update/) has the commands.

## Recovery

An interrupted flash leaves an invalid CRC; the bootloader refuses to start the firmware and waits, so the board is
not lost: flash again. A board that answers nothing at all: power-cycle it with the host already polling, to catch
the 2 s window. The one thing the tools refuse, and that would need a programming adapter to undo, is flashing an
image linked for `0x08000000` (a firmware from the `main` branch) over the firmware region.

## Installing it

Boards shipped with firmware 104 or older have no bootloader. [Installing the bootloader on an older board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/07-firmware/bootloader/)
puts it there once, with a programming adapter at `0x08000000`; from then on the board updates like any other.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/07-firmware/update/ -->

# Updating through the bootloader

A driver with the bootloader (firmware 105 or newer) is updated over the UART connector or the CAN bus: the host
tells the driver to reset, the bootloader waits two seconds for a host, and the host streams the new image into it.
No programming adapter, and nothing to open.

!!! warning "Before you update"
    - Park the mechanism: the motor loses torque during the update and until the new firmware is calibrated and
      commanded.
    - An update may clear the calibration (the release notes say so when it does); plan to calibrate and `#Save`
      afterwards, and note the gains `#Info` prints.
    - On a bus with several drivers, update each node; a bus with mixed releases behaves unpredictably.

## With Motor GUI

[Motor GUI](https://motorgui.com/) in Chrome or Edge, connected over the serial adapter or the CANvas adapter:
choose the release, and the GUI fetches the image and its manifest from the GitHub release, verifies the size and
the SHA-256, resets the driver into its bootloader and flashes it. This is the way for one driver on the bench.

## With the bootloader's command-line tool

The [bootloader repository](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/stm32f103c-bootloader) has `host_tools/bl_flash.py`,
which flashes an image over CAN (slcan or candleLight/gs_usb adapters) or over UART:

```
cd host_tools
pip install -r requirements.txt

# over CAN with a CANvas (slcan) adapter on COM6, driver with board ID 0
python bl_flash.py --transport can --can-interface slcan --channel COM6 flash spectral-bldc-firmware-V107.bin --board 0 --erase-first

# over UART on COM7
python bl_flash.py --transport uart --port COM7 --baudrate 256000 flash spectral-bldc-firmware-V107.bin --board 0 --erase-first
```

The tool sends the reset command to the running firmware (`#Reset` over UART, Send_Reset over CAN), catches the
bootloader's two-second window, erases the application pages and streams the image page by page, each page
verified by a CRC; `list` shows the boards in bootloader mode, `set-id` changes a board's bootloader ID. The image
is the `spectral-bldc-firmware-V<number>.bin` from the GitHub release.

!!! note "Board ID and node ID"
    The bootloader has its own board ID (0 to 13), kept in its configuration page, separate from the firmware's
    CAN node ID. The firmware keeps the two in step when the node ID is set (`#CANID`, Send_CAN_ID), so a driver's
    bootloader ID is normally its node ID.

## From a PAR6 control box

A robot built on the Robot Control Box updates every joint from the box itself, over its own CAN bus, from the
dashboard's Firmware tab or with `tools/flash_motor_firmware.py`; the
[PAR6 documentation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/par6/) describes it.

## What happens in the driver

1. The host sends the reset; the firmware reboots into the bootloader.
2. The bootloader listens for two seconds. With no host it starts the firmware; with a host it stays as long as
   the host keeps talking (60 s during a flash).
3. The application pages are erased, then written page by page; each page is checked by a CRC.
4. The bootloader checks the whole image's CRC, records it, and starts the new firmware.

## When it fails

A flash that fails or is cancelled part way is not a brick: the stored CRC is invalid, so the bootloader refuses to
start the firmware and waits for a host. Run the flash again; `bl_flash.py list` (or a passive scan from the
control box) finds the board. A board that answers nothing: power-cycle it with the host already polling, to catch
the two-second window.

An image linked for `0x08000000` (a firmware from the `main` branch, release 104 and earlier) must never be
flashed through the bootloader: it would overwrite the bootloader's own region if the tool did not refuse it.
The tools validate the image first.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/07-firmware/bootloader/ -->

# Installing the bootloader on an older board

A driver running firmware 104 or older has no bootloader: its firmware starts at the beginning of the flash. To
run any release from 105 on, which is linked to start above the bootloader, the bootloader must be installed
once, with a programming adapter on the JTAG connector. After that, every update goes over UART or CAN.

!!! warning
    Disconnect the motor supply and the UART adapter before connecting the programming adapter. The adapter
    powers the board at 3.3 V.

## What you need

- The [programming adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/jtag-programming-adapter-1-27-pitch) (an ST-LINK
  with the 1.27 mm pogo-pin adapter for the JTAG pads), or any ST-LINK, J-Link or OpenOCD-compatible probe wired
  to 3.3 V, GND, SWDIO and SWCLK.
- [STM32CubeProgrammer](https://www.st.com/en/development-tools/stm32cubeprog.html) or the older
  [STM32 ST-LINK Utility](https://www.st.com/en/development-tools/stsw-link004.html) on the PC, with the
  [ST-LINK drivers](https://www.st.com/en/development-tools/stsw-link009.html).
- The bootloader binary from the [bootloader repository's `bin/` folder](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/stm32f103c-bootloader/tree/main/bin);
  its `README.md` names the current file.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![The programming adapter on the JTAG pads](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/FLASHING2-Photoroom.webp){ width="520" }
  <figcaption>Figure 18: The JTAG pads. The adapter is pressed onto them; a little pressure makes the contact.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Steps

1. Connect the adapter to the JTAG pads and the PC.
2. In the programmer, connect to the target (SWD). The STM32F103CB shows up with 128 KB of flash.
3. Erase the chip, or at least the application region: the old firmware and the bootloader must not overlap.
4. Program the bootloader binary at address **`0x08000000`**.
5. Disconnect the adapter, power the driver. The bootloader finds no valid application and waits in bootloader
   mode (the LED stays off).
6. Flash the firmware release through the bootloader, over UART or CAN, as in
   [Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/07-firmware/update/).
7. `#Info` shows the new release. `#Default`, enter the motor parameters, calibrate, `#Save`.

!!! note "Memory layout"
    `0x08000000`–`0x080022FF` bootloader, `0x08002C00` its configuration page (board ID, the application's CRC),
    `0x08003000`–`0x0801FFFF` the application (116 KB). The bootloader keeps a magic value in RAM to hand over
    to the application in about 10 ms on a normal boot.

## The programmer's settings

In ST-LINK Utility, *Target → Settings* with SWD and the default frequency works; *Target → Program & Verify*
with the start address `0x08000000`. The pictures of the old flashing procedure apply to the connection and the
settings dialog:

| Settings | Programming |
|---|---|
| ![ST-LINK settings](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/stlink1.webp){ width="420" } | ![ST-LINK program and verify](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/stlink_prog.webp){ width="420" } |

The same adapter uploads a firmware you build yourself, see [Building from source](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/07-firmware/building/).

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/07-firmware/building/ -->

# Building from source

The firmware is a PlatformIO project for the Arduino core on the STM32F103CB, in the `Spectral BLDC Firmware` folder
of the [firmware repository](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-Micro-BLDC-controller/tree/Bootloader_main/Spectral%20BLDC%20Firmware)
on the `Bootloader_main` branch.

## Building

1. Install [Visual Studio Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/download) and the PlatformIO extension.
2. Clone the repository and check out `Bootloader_main`.
3. Open the `Spectral BLDC Firmware` folder in VS Code; PlatformIO fetches the platform (`ststm32@15.4.1`) and builds
   with the PlatformIO *Build* button or `pio run`. The image is `.pio/build/genericSTM32F103CB/firmware.bin`.

The project is linked for the bootloader: `VECT_TAB_OFFSET=0x3000`, the linker script `ldscript_bootloader.ld`,
the upload offset `0x08003000` and a maximum size of 118784 bytes, in `platformio.ini`. A build that exceeds the
size fails to link.

## Uploading

- **Through the bootloader**: flash the built `firmware.bin` with `bl_flash.py` or Motor GUI as in
  [Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/07-firmware/update/). This is how a release is installed, and works on any driver with
  the bootloader.
- **With the programming adapter**: *Upload* in PlatformIO uses ST-LINK and writes the image at `0x08003000`. The
  bootloader must already be on the board; the upload does not touch it. The serial monitor (the plug icon) opens
  the UART at 256000 with `send_on_enter`, so you can type commands to the driver from the same window.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Upload in VS Code](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/VSUPLOAD.png){ width="700" }
  <figcaption>Figure 19: Build, upload and the serial monitor in PlatformIO's status bar.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Where things are

| | |
|---|---|
| `src/constants.h` | `FIRMWARE_VERSION`, the CAN command IDs, the EEPROM map, the loop and PWM frequencies |
| `src/common.h` | the controller and PID structures with their defaults |
| `src/communication.cpp` | the UART command handlers |
| `src/communication_CAN.cpp` | the CAN receive switch and the transmit functions |
| `src/SerialPacketParser.cpp` | the UART parser and the list of names it accepts |
| `src/motor_control.cpp` | the control loops, the calibration routine, the gripper state machine |
| `src/bootloader_config.cpp` | the vector table offset and the reset into the bootloader |
| `release_guide.md` | how a release is cut: version bump, build, tag, GitHub release with `firmware.json` |

## Making a release

`release_guide.md` in the repository is the procedure: bump `FIRMWARE_VERSION`, build, commit the source change
with the rebuilt `Binaries/firmware.bin`, tag `V<number>`, create the GitHub release with the image and
`firmware.json` and the release notes. This site's `tools/sync_firmware.py` reads a release by its tag; the
version box names the release.

## A firmware for a board without a bootloader

The `main` branch builds a firmware linked at `0x08000000` for boards that have no bootloader. It stops at release 104 and is not maintained; install the bootloader instead,
[Installing the bootloader on an older board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/07-firmware/bootloader/).
