| [`#Term`](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/utility/) | Set/Get | int | Status and utility |
| [`#Tlim`](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/utility/) | Set/Get | int | Status and utility |
| [`#Ud`](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/motion/) | Set/Get | int | Motion |
| [`#Uq`](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/motion/) | Set/Get | int | Motion |
| [`#V`](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/motion/) | Set/Get | int | Motion |
| [`#Vbus`](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/utility/) | Get |  | Status and utility |
| [`#Vlim`](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/gains/) | Set/Get | int | Gains and limits |
| [`#Vlimit`](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/gains/) | Set/Get | int | Gains and limits |
| [`#Vmax`](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/utility/) | Set/Get | int | Status and utility |
| [`#Vp`](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/calibration/) | Set/Get | int | Calibration and motor parameters |

The parser also accepts `#Calangle`, `#EN`, `#SIN`, `#SPWM`, `#Vmin`, `#flux`, `#zz`, which have no handler: the driver answers nothing to them.

## By group

- [Motion](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/motion/): setpoints and modes
- [Gains and limits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/gains/): the loop gains, the limits, the integrator reset, the current loop bandwidth
- [Calibration and motor parameters](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/calibration/): `Cal`, the motor's R, L and pole pairs, the constants calibration finds, the calibration settings
- [Status and utility](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/utility/): save, reset, defaults, identity, errors, temperature, the cyclic output
- [Gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/gripper/): gripper mode


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/motion/ -->

# Motion

| Command | Kind | Argument | What it does | Response |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `#Iq` | Set/Get | float: current setpoint in mA | Current (torque) control with the given Iq setpoint. Enters **current** mode. | the measured Iq in mA |
| `#Id` | Set/Get | float: current setpoint in mA | Sets the Id setpoint; normally left at 0. | the measured Id in mA |
| `#Uq` | Set/Get | int: voltage in mV | Voltage-torque mode with the given q-axis voltage (no current loop). Enters **voltage torque** mode. | the Uq setpoint in mV |
| `#Ud` | Set/Get | int: voltage in mV | The d-axis voltage used in voltage-torque mode; does not change the mode. Enters **gripper** mode. | the Ud setpoint in mV |
| `#V` | Set/Get | int: speed setpoint in encoder ticks/s | Velocity control with the given speed. Enters **velocity** mode. | the measured speed in ticks/s |
| `#P` | Set/Get | int: position setpoint in encoder ticks | Position control to the given position. Enters **position** mode. | the measured position in ticks |
| `#PD` | Set/Get | int: position setpoint in encoder ticks | Impedance (PD) control around the given position with the gains KP and KD. Enters **PD** mode. | the measured position in ticks |
| `#PDV` | Set/Get | int: speed setpoint in encoder ticks/s | The speed setpoint of the PD loop. | the PD speed setpoint |
| `#PDI` | Set/Get | int: current feedforward in mA | The current feedforward of the PD loop. | the PD current feedforward |
| `#Idle` | Action |  | Goes to idle; the motor coasts or brakes as set by Brake. Enters **idle** mode. | `Idle` |
| `#Brake` | Set/Get | int: 0 or 1 | What the motor does in idle: 1 brakes (the phases are shorted through the driver), 0 coasts (the phases are open). Takes effect once the driver is idle, so send Idle first. Added in firmware 107. | the setting |
| `#Close` | Action |  | Leaves open loop and goes back to closed-loop idle. Enters **idle** mode. | nothing |
| `#Openloop` | Set/Get | float: electrical speed | Turns the stator field at the given electrical speed without the encoder in the loop, with the voltage set by Openv. Enters **open loop** mode. | the open-loop speed |


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/gains/ -->

# Gains and limits

| Command | Kind | Argument | What it does | Response |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `#Vlim` | Set/Get | int: voltage in mV | The voltage limit of the current loops (Ud and Uq); 0 means use the supply voltage. | the current limit in mV |
| `#Vlimit` | Set/Get | int: speed in encoder ticks/s | The speed limit; the velocity integrator is clamped to it. | the current limit |
| `#Kpp` | Set/Get | float: gain | Kp of the position loop. | the current value |
| `#KP` | Set/Get | float: gain | KP of the impedance (PD) loop. | the current value |
| `#KD` | Set/Get | float: gain | KD of the impedance (PD) loop. | the current value |
| `#Kpv` | Set/Get | float: gain | Kp of the velocity loop. | the current value |
| `#Kpiq` | Set/Get | float: gain | Kp of the Iq current loop; also sets Kpid. | the current value |
| `#Kpid` | Set/Get | float: gain | Kp of the Id current loop. | the current value |
| `#Kiv` | Set/Get | float: gain | Ki of the velocity loop. | the current value |
| `#Kiiq` | Set/Get | float: gain | Ki of the Iq current loop; also sets Kiid. | the current value |
| `#Kiid` | Set/Get | float: gain | Ki of the Id current loop. | the current value |
| `#Ilim` | Set/Get | int: current in mA | The Iq current limit. Set it to the rated phase current of your motor; the firmware clamps it to 2800 mA. | the current limit |
| `#Cbw` | Set/Get | float: bandwidth in Hz | The current loop bandwidth calibration uses to compute Kpiq and Kiiq. | the bandwidth |
| `#Rstint` | Set/Get | int: 0 or 1 | Whether the integral accumulators are reset on every new setpoint. | the setting |


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/calibration/ -->

# Calibration and motor parameters

| Command | Kind | Argument | What it does | Response |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `#R` | Set/Get | float: resistance in Ω | The phase resistance of the motor, measured by Cal; it can also be set by hand. | the current value |
| `#L` | Set/Get | float: inductance in H | The phase inductance of the motor, measured by Cal; it can also be set by hand. | the current value |
| `#Kt` | Set/Get | float: Nm/A | The torque constant, found by calibration. | the current value |
| `#KV` | Set/Get | float: rpm/V | The velocity constant, found by calibration. | the current value |
| `#Flux` | Set/Get | float: Wb | The flux linkage, found by calibration. Not reachable over UART: the parser accepts `#flux` (lowercase) but the handler expects `Flux`, so neither spelling works. | the current value |
| `#Cal` | Action |  | Runs the calibration routine (see Calibration): it measures R and L, finds the pole pairs, the phase order and the angle offset, and measures Kt, KV and the flux linkage. | the calibration log |
| `#Offset` | Set/Get | float: angle in rad | The angle offset between encoder zero and electrical zero, found by calibration. | the current value |
| `#Iqoffset` | Set/Get | int: current in mA | The current used by the angle-offset search. | the current value |
| `#Magnet` | Get |  | Reads the encoder's magnet status. | `Magnet Good` or `Magnet Bad` |
| `#Dir` | Set/Get | int: 0 or 1 | The counting direction of the encoder (1 is the default). | the current value |
| `#Phase` | Get |  | Prints the phase order found by calibration. | `Phase order is: N` |
| `#Resv` | Set/Get | int: voltage in mV | The voltage the resistance test of Cal starts at; it rises until the power reaches Calpwr. | the current value |
| `#Calpwr` | Set/Get | float: power in W | The power the resistance and inductance tests of Cal may dissipate in the motor. | the current value |
| `#Openv` | Set/Get | int: voltage in mV | The voltage of the open-loop spin, in calibration and with Openloop. | the current value |
| `#Opens` | Set/Get | float: electrical speed in rad/s | The speed of the open-loop spin in calibration. | the current value |
| `#Vp` | Set/Get | int: voltage in mV | The voltage of the phase-order search in calibration. | the current value |
| `#Calibrated` | Set/Get | int: 0 or 1 | The calibrated flag. `#Calibrated 1` clears a calibration error without calibrating; the motor may still be uncalibrated. | the flag |
| `#PP` | Set/Get | int: pole pairs | The motor's pole pairs, found by Cal; they can also be set by hand. | the current value |


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/utility/ -->

# Status and utility

| Command | Kind | Argument | What it does | Response |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `#Vmax` | Set/Get | int: voltage in mV | The supply voltage above which a Vbus error is raised. | `Vmax in mV: N` |
| `#Save` | Action |  | Writes the configuration to the EEPROM. Do it after calibration and after tuning. | `Save` |
| `#Reset` | Action |  | Resets the driver. From firmware 105 the reset lands in the bootloader, which waits 2 s for a flashing host and then starts the firmware again. | nothing |
| `#Tlim` | Set/Get | int: temperature in °C | The temperature at which the temperature error is raised; 75 by default. | `Temp limit N` |
| `#Default` | Action |  | Writes the factory defaults to the EEPROM, including the serial number, hardware version and batch date, and clears the gripper flag, heartbeat and watchdog. Back those up first. | `Loaded default config!` |
| `#Temp` | Get |  | Prints the thermistor temperature. | °C, or `Temp Off` while the thermistor is disabled |
| `#Term` | Set/Get | int: 0 or 1 | Enables the thermistor measurement and the temperature error (off by default). | the setting |
| `#Mode` | Get |  | Prints the control mode. | `Idle mode`, `Position control`, `Speed control`, `Current control`, `PD control`, `Open loop`, `Gripper mode`, `Gripper calib mode` |
| `#Vbus` | Get |  | Prints the supply voltage. | mV |
| `#Error` | Get |  | Prints which errors are active. | `No errors!` or `In error state!` followed by one line per active error |
| `#Clear` | Action |  | Clears the errors and goes to idle. An error whose cause is still present comes straight back; a calibration error is cleared only by calibrating (or `#Calibrated 1`). Enters **idle** mode. | `Clear errors` |
| `#Iabc` | Get |  | Prints the phase currents. | `Ia`, `Ib` in mA |
| `#PWM` | Get |  | Prints the PWM duty values. | the duties |
| `#Help` | Action |  | Prints a short command reference. Added in firmware 106. | the reference |
| `#Info` | Get |  | Prints the driver's identity and state: hardware and firmware version, serial number, motor parameters, calibration, errors. | the report |
| `#Param` | Get |  | Prints every gain of every loop. | the gains |
| `#Cyc` | Set/Get | int: interval in ms (0 = off) | Sends position, speed and Iq on its own every interval: `$ <position> <speed> <Iq>`; for BetterSerialPlotter. | `Cyclic disabled` when turned off |
| `#Cyca` | Set/Get | int: interval in ms (0 = off) | Like Cyc, in the Arduino plotter format `Position:x,Speed:y,Iq:z`. | `Cyclic disabled` when turned off |
| `#CANID` | Set/Get | int: 0 to 13 | The CAN node ID. Use 0 to 13: the firmware accepts 14 and 15, but the bootloader reserves them and a driver on one of those cannot be updated over CAN. Setting the ID also sets the bootloader's board ID. Kept over a power cycle after Save. | the ID, or `Invalid CAN ID` |
| `#SERNUM` | Set/Get | int: number | The serial number stored in the EEPROM. | `Serial number is: N` |
| `#Activate` | Action |  | Sets the activated flag. | `Controller activated` |
| `#Pullconfig` | Get |  | Prints the whole configuration on one line, for Motor GUI. | the configuration |
| `#LED` | Set/Get | int: 0 or 1 | Turns the status LED on or off. | the LED state |


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/uart/gripper/ -->

# Gripper

| Command | Kind | Argument | What it does | Response |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `#Gripper` | Set/Get | int: 0 or 1 | Whether this driver is a gripper. Save it; `#Default` clears it. | the flag |
| `#Gripcal` | Action |  | Starts the gripper calibration (the jaws find their end stops). Enters **gripper calibration** mode. | `Gripper calibration!` |
| `#Gripinfo` | Get |  | Prints the gripper state: calibrated, activated, end stops, position, current. | the report |
| `#Gripstop` | Set/Get | int: 0 or 1 | The gripper E-stop bit. | the bit |
| `#Gripact` | Set/Get | int: 0 or 1 | The activate bit. | the bit |
| `#Gripcur` | Set/Get | int: current in mA | The current limit of gripper moves. The firmware does not clamp it; see the gripper manual for the safe range. | the setpoint |
| `#Gripvel` | Set/Get | int: 0 to 255 | The speed setpoint of gripper moves. | the setpoint |
| `#Grippos` | Set/Get | int: 0 (open) to 255 (closed) | The position setpoint; also activates the gripper, sets the action bit and goes to gripper mode. Enters **gripper** mode. | the current position |


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/defaults/ -->

# Defaults

The values the firmware starts with, from its source (`common.h`) at the release this site describes. `#Default` writes the EEPROM defaults, which are the same unless the firmware comment says otherwise.

| Variable | Default | Firmware comment |
|---|---|---|
| `SERIAL_NUMBER` | 1 |  |
| `HARDWARE_VERSION` | 1 | Version of the Spectral BLDC driver PCB |
| `BATCH_DATE` | 1 | Date the batch was produced |
| `SOFTWARE_VERSION` | 1 | Software release |
| `I_AM_GRIPPER` | 1 | Is motor controller gripper (1) or not (0) |
| `LED_ON_OFF` | 1 | Use LED for status indication |
| `interrupt_tick` | 0 | Ticks of our interrupt routine |
| `TEMP_DEG` | 23 | Temperature in degrees celsius |
| `theta_offset` | 0.0f | will be determined at calibration |
| `pole_pairs` | 11 | Number of pole pairs of your BLDC motor |
| `current_control_bandwidth` | 500 | default 200 HZ; Will set PI gains for Q and D current loops based on phase resistance |
| `sleep_pin_state` | 0 |  |
| `reset_pin_state` | 0 |  |
| `Crossover_frequency` | 0.0 | Crossover frequency, in Radians per sample |
| `DIR_` | 1 | When looking at the magnetic encoder counter-clockwise is POSITIVE rotation. |
| `Phase_order` | 2 |  |
| `commutation_dir` | 1 | +1 or -1, auto-detected at calibration so +Iq/+velocity/+rotation map to +encoder rotation |
| `Thermistor_on_off` | 0 | Are we taking termistor mesurements? 0 is off, 1 is on |
| `Controller_mode` | 0 | 0 -> idle, 1 -> Positon, 2 -> Speed, 3 -> Current, 4 -> PD, 5 -> Open-loop speed, 6 -> Gripper mode, 7-> Calibrate gripper, 8 -> Voltage Torque mode |
| `brake_coast` | 0 | Idle-mode (Controller_mode == 0) phase behavior: 0 = coast (driver disabled, Hi-Z), 1 = brake (driver stays enabled, zero-voltage PWM vector shorts the phases together) |
| `Resistance` | 0 | Resistance of SINGLE PHASE of your BLDC motor |
| `Total_Resistance` | 0 | = 2 * Resistance + 2 * R_sense + 2 *Rdson |
| `Inductance` | 0 | Inductance of SINGLE PHASE of your BLDC motor |
| `Kt` | 0 | Torque constant of your BLDC motor |
| `flux_linkage` | 0 | Flux linkage of your BLDC motor |
| `KV` | 0 |  |
| `Max_temperature` | 75 | Max temperature in degrees |
| `Min_temperature` | -20 | Min temperature in degrees |
| `Max_Vbus` | 29500 | Max vbus voltage in mV |
| `Min_Vbus` | 9000 | Min vbus voltage in mV |
| `execution_time` | 0 | Execution time of our interrupt loops |
| `watchdog_time_ms` | 0 |  |
| `watchdog_reset` | 1 |  |
| `watchdog_action` | 0 | Hold position, Idle, brake |
| `Heartbeat_rate_ms` | 0 | Motor controller will send data every Heartbeat_rate_ms |
| `Send_heartbeat` | 0 |  |
| `Activated` | 0 | If controller is activated or not |
| `Error` | 0 | General error |
| `temperature_error` | 0 | Termistor reported error |
| `encoder_error` | 0 | Encoder magnet is not alligned error |
| `Vbus_error` | 0 | Vbus voltage is too small or too large |
| `Driver_error` | 0 | Driver reported error. 3 possible conditions: Undervoltage, thermal shutdown, overcurrent |
| `Velocity_error` | 0 | We are moving too fast |
| `Current_error` | 0 | We go past max current |
| `ESTOP_error` | 0 | If we received estop command |
| `Watchdog_error` | 0 | If we pass watchdog timeout time |
| `CAN_init_error` | 0 | Set if CAN peripheral failed to initialize; CAN bus is skipped, UART stays usable |
| `commutation` | 0 | 0 is space vector, 1 is sine |
| `Calibration` | 0 | 0 - outside of calibration, 1 inside of calibration, 2 failed calibration, 3 success calibration |
| `Calibrated` | 0 | 0 if motor is not calibrated, 1 if it is calibrated |
| `Resistance_calc_voltage` | 1000 | Voltage used to calculate resistance //1000 |
| `Calibration_power` | 12 | Max power that can dissipate during inductance test. |
| `Calibration_Inductance_voltage` | 0 | Calculated from Calibration power and resistance |
| `Open_loop_voltage` | 5000 | Voltage to use when spinning the motor open loop. In mV |
| `Open_loop_speed` | 20.0 | Speed to be used when spinning the motor open loop. In RAD/s |
| `Number_of_rotations` | 8 | Number of open loop electrical rotations during calibration |
| `Phase_voltage` | 5000 | Max voltage to be used during Kv calculation |
| `Calib_error` | 0 |  |

| `KV_status` | 0 |  |
| `cyclic` | 0 | If 1 we Periodically send messages without request from host. |
| `cyclic_a` | 0 | If 1 we Periodically send messages without request from host. |
| `cyclic_period` | 0 | We send messages every cyclic_period |
| `CAN_ID` | 0 | CAN id of THIS motor driver! No 2 motor drivers can share the same ID. |
| `Wrong_DL` | 0 |  |

# Errors and LED states

## The LED

| Pattern | State |
|---|---|
| three short flashes, a pause | normal operation: calibrated, no error |
| flashing every 0.5 s | calibration running |
| on, steady | error mode, or not calibrated |
| off | no power, or `#LED 0` |

| Normal operation | Calibration | Error mode |
|---|---|---|
| ![Three short flashes and a pause](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/Normal.webp){ width="180" } | ![Flashing every 0.5 s](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/Calib.webp){ width="180" } | ![On, steady](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/Error2.webp){ width="180" } |

## The error flags

The flags as the firmware keeps them, the line `#Error` prints for each, and where each sits in the two bytes of
Send_Respond_State_of_Errors (bits numbered from the most significant).

| Flag | `#Error` prints | Byte, bit | Raised when |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Error` | `In error state!` | 0, 7 | any of the flags below is set (also the error bit of every CAN identifier) |
| `temperature_error` | `Temp error` | 0, 6 | the thermistor reads above `#Tlim` (with `#Term 1`) |
| `encoder_error` | `Encoder error` | 0, 5 | the magnet is not detected or the reading fails its check |
| `Vbus_error` | `Vbus error` | 0, 4 | the supply is below 9 V or above `#Vmax` (29.5 V by default) |
| `Driver_error` | `Driver error (undervoltage, thermal shutdown, or overcurrent)` | 0, 3 | the MOSFET driver's fault output is active |
| `Velocity_error` | `Velocity error` | 0, 2 | the speed exceeds the limit |
| `Current_error` | `Current error` | 0, 1 | never in this firmware; reserved |
| `ESTOP_error` | `Received ESTOP command` | 0, 0 | Send_ESTOP was received |
| `Calibrated` (0) | `Not calibrated` | 1, 7 (1 = calibrated) | the motor has not been calibrated |
| `Activated` | — | 1, 6 | the activated flag, not an error |
| `Watchdog_error` | `Watchdog error` | 1, 5 | the watchdog time passed without a valid CAN frame |

Gripper mode has its own flags in Respond_Gripper_data_pack: a temperature error, a timeout error (the jaw did
not reach its target in time) and an E-stop error; see the [Gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/gripper/) reference.

## Clearing

`#Clear` and Send_Clear_Error clear every flag except `Calibrated` and go to idle; a flag whose cause persists is
set again at once. The watchdog, E-stop and velocity errors clear and stay clear; the Vbus, encoder, driver and
temperature errors come back until the cause is gone. Calibration clears the calibration error.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/python/ -->

# Python library

The `Spectral-BLDC` package ([Spectral-BLDC-Python](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-Python),
`pip install Spectral-BLDC`) has one method per CAN message in `Spectral_BLDC.SpectralCAN`, and
`Spectral_BLDC.CanCommunication` for the bus. [With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/06-operation/python/) shows how they are used.

## Calls and messages

| Library call | Sends | Answered with | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Send_data_pack_1()` | Send_data_pack_1 (ID 2) | Respond_data_pack_1 | [Motion](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/motion/#send_data_pack_1) |
| `Send_data_pack_PD()` | Send_data_pack_PD (ID 4) | Respond_data_pack_1 | [Motion](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/motion/#send_data_pack_pd) |
| `Send_PD_Gains()` | Send_PD_Gains (ID 16) | — | [Gains and limits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/gains-and-limits/#send_pd_gains) |
| `Send_Current_Gains()` | Send_Current_Gains (ID 17) | — | [Gains and limits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/gains-and-limits/#send_current_gains) |
| `Send_Velocity_Gains()` | Send_Velocity_Gains (ID 18) | — | [Gains and limits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/gains-and-limits/#send_velocity_gains) |
| `Send_Position_Gains()` | Send_Position_Gains (ID 19) | — | [Gains and limits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/gains-and-limits/#send_position_gains) |
| `Send_Limits()` | Send_Limits (ID 20) | — | [Gains and limits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/gains-and-limits/#send_limits) |
| `Send_Kt()` | Send_Kt (ID 22) | — | [Gains and limits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/gains-and-limits/#send_kt) |
| `Send_Voltage_Limit()` | Send_Voltage_Limit (ID 34) | — | [Gains and limits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/gains-and-limits/#send_voltage_limit) |
| `Send_Respond_Ping()` | Send_Respond_Ping (ID 10) | Send_Respond_Ping (data frame) | [Status requests](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/status/#send_respond_ping) |
| `Send_Respond_Temperature()` | Send_Respond_Temperature (ID 23) | Send_Respond_Temperature (data frame) | [Status requests](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/status/#send_respond_temperature) |
| `Send_Respond_Voltage()` | Send_Respond_Voltage (ID 24) | Send_Respond_Voltage (data frame) | [Status requests](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/status/#send_respond_voltage) |
| `Send_Respond_Device_Info()` | Send_Respond_Device_Info (ID 25) | Send_Respond_Device_Info (data frame) | [Status requests](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/status/#send_respond_device_info) |
| `Send_Respond_State_of_Errors()` | Send_Respond_State_of_Errors (ID 26) | Send_Respond_State_of_Errors (data frame) | [Status requests](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/status/#send_respond_state_of_errors) |
| `Send_Respond_Iq_data()` | Send_Respond_Iq_data (ID 27) | Send_Respond_Iq_data (data frame) | [Status requests](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/status/#send_respond_iq_data) |
| `Send_Respond_Encoder_data()` | Send_Respond_Encoder_data (ID 28) | Send_Respond_Encoder_data (data frame) | [Status requests](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/status/#send_respond_encoder_data) |
| `Send_Respond_Kt()` | Send_Respond_Kt (ID 33) | Send_Respond_Kt (data frame) | [Status requests](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/status/#send_respond_kt) |
| `Send_CAN_ID()` | Send_CAN_ID (ID 11) | — | [System](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/system/#send_can_id) |
| `Send_ESTOP()` | Send_ESTOP (ID 0) | — | [System](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/system/#send_estop) |
| `Send_Idle()` | Send_Idle (ID 12) | — | [System](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/system/#send_idle) |

| `Send_Reset()` | Send_Reset (ID 14) | — | [System](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/system/#send_reset) |
| `Send_Clear_Error()` | Send_Clear_Error (ID 1) | — | [System](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/system/#send_clear_error) |
| `Send_Watchdog()` | Send_Watchdog (ID 15) | — | [System](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/system/#send_watchdog) |
| `Send_Heartbeat_Setup()` | Send_Heartbeat_Setup (ID 30) | — | [System](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/system/#send_heartbeat_setup) |
| `Send_gripper_data_pack()` | Send_gripper_data_pack (ID 61) | Respond_Gripper_data_pack | [Gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/gripper/#send_gripper_data_pack) |
| `Send_gripper_calibrate()` | Send_gripper_calibrate (ID 62) | — | [Gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/reference/can/gripper/#send_gripper_calibrate) |

## Receiving

`CanCommunication.receive_can_messages(timeout)` returns `(message, ids)`: the raw `python-can` message and a tuple
`ids` with `node_id`, `command_id` and `error_bit` from the identifier, or `(None, None)` after the timeout.
`SpectralCAN.UnpackData(message, ids)` decodes the message into the object's attributes:

| Message | Attributes |
|---|---|
| Respond_data_pack_1 | `position`, `speed`, `current` |

| Send_Respond_Encoder_data | `position`, `speed` |
| Send_Respond_Iq_data | `current` |
| Send_Respond_Temperature | `temperature` |
| Send_Respond_Voltage | `voltage` |
| Send_Respond_Device_Info | `HARDWARE_VERSION`, `BATCH_DATE`, `SOFTWARE_VERSION`, `SERIAL_NUMBER` |
| Send_Respond_State_of_Errors | `error`, `temperature_error`, `encoder_error`, `vbus_error`, `driver_error`, `velocity_error`, `current_error`, `estop_error`, `calibrated`, `activated`, `watchdog_error` |
| Send_Respond_Kt | `Kt` |
| Respond_Gripper_data_pack | `gripper_position`, `gripper_current`, `gripper_activated`, `gripper_action_status`, `gripper_object_detection`, `gripper_temperature_error`, `gripper_timeout_error`, `gripper_estop_error`, `gripper_calibrated` |

!!! note "Object detection in the library"
    Library version 1.20 assembles `gripper_object_detection` with the two bits swapped relative to the firmware,
    so it reports 1 where the gripper sends 2 (object detected while opening) and 2 where it sends 1 (object
    detected while closing); 0 and 3 are unaffected. Until the library is fixed, swap the two values in your
    program, or read the bits yourself from the frame.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/guides/ -->

# Guides

Worked examples with code, from a first Python program to a mobile robot, a leg, a gravity-compensated arm and two
motors coupled over a network, and the SimpleFOC library as an alternative firmware. The CAN commands and the Python
library are the same on STEPFOC, so the code runs there unchanged.

- [Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/guides/python/): read a driver's position and speed over CAN
- [Mobile robot](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/guides/mobile-robot/): two wheels driven from a game controller
- [Quadruped leg](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/guides/quadruped/): the kinematics and control of a two-motor leg
- [Gravity compensation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/guides/gravity-compensation/): hold a link against gravity with a current feedforward
- [Bilateral teleoperation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/guides/bilateral-teleoperation/): two motors that follow each other, with force feedback
- [SimpleFOC](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/guides/simplefoc/): running the SimpleFOC library on the Spectral Micro instead of the Spectral firmware

More examples are in the [Spectral-BLDC-Python examples](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-Python/tree/main/examples).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/guides/python/ -->

# Python guide

More examples are in the [Spectral-BLDC-Python examples folder](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-Python/tree/main/examples).

## Examples

Check the examples [here!](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-Python/tree/main/examples)

``` py title="Get_encoder_data.py"
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
import time

# Init comms channel 
Communication1 = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM41', bitrate=1000000)
# Init motor object
Motor1 = Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=Communication1)

while True:

    # Send this msg to the motor controller, it will respond with position and speed data
    Motor1.Send_Respond_Encoder_data()

    # Get CAN msg, timeout tells us to continue if there is no msg after in this case 0.2 s
    message, UnpackedMessageID = Communication1.receive_can_messages(timeout=0.2) 

    # If there was a msg unpack it
    if message is not None:
        print(f"Message is: {message}")
        print(f"Node ID is : {UnpackedMessageID.node_id}")
        print(f"Message ID is: {UnpackedMessageID.command_id}")
        print(f"Error bit is: {UnpackedMessageID.error_bit}")
        print(f"Message length is: {message.dlc}")
        print(f"Is is remote frame: {message.is_remote_frame}")
        print(f"Timestamp is: {message.timestamp}")
        
        # Here we unpack the data from the packet
        Motor1.UnpackData(message,UnpackedMessageID)
        # We are interested in position and speed data that was requested by calling Send_Respond_Encoder_data
        print(f"Motor position is: {Motor1.position}")
        print(f"Motor speed is: {Motor1.speed}")

    else:
        print("No message after timeout period!")
    print("")
    time.sleep(1 )
```

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/guides/mobile-robot/ -->

# Mobile robot guide

## Intro
This guide is a really simple example on how you can control mobile robot based on **spectral micro BLDC drives** using xbox controller! <br />

**By following this guide you will be able to make something like this: [Link!](https://youtu.be/LGMLyr4dZZ0)**

!!! tip "Python API"
    This guide leverages [Spectral BLDC python API](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-Python/tree/main)

What you will need to create a simple mobile robot is:

* 2 x spectral micro BLDC - used for 2 wheels 
* Wires to connect everything up: [CAN wires](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-can-cable), [Power wires](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-power-cable)
* 2 x BLDC motors
* 1 x [CAN adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/canvas-usb-to-can-adapter)
* 1 x Drill battery adapter: [Example](https://s.click.aliexpress.com/e/_DExmYtl) - This is great way to power your BLDC motors with cheap and affordable batteries
* A Laptop or raspberry pi
* Xbox controller

!!! note "Building the robot"
    In this guide we only recommend you the hardware you can use to build the robot you designed. We do not offer already made designs you can build!

## Setup

![drawing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/AMR_setup.webp)

The setup will be the same for any kind of mobile robot. You will need to follow the  diagram above to wire everything up.

* First you need to calibrate your Spectral BLDC drivers with the motors you are using. 
* After that change the CAN ids of one of the drivers to CAN 1. You can do it by using UART commands: #CANID 1 and after that #Save
* Now connect CAN adapters CAN bus to one of the drivers and then from that driver connect to the second driver. Make sure that last driver in chain has its CAN termination resistor in "ON" state
* Connect the power to both drivers. You can daisy chain it or use 2 separate wires.
* You will also need to connect your xbox controller to the PC/laptop via Bluetooth.

The code below is really simple example that drives the robot using the left joystick of the controller.

``` py title="Spectral_mobile_robot_xbox.py"
from inputs import get_gamepad
import math
import threading
import time
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral

Communication1 = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM3', bitrate=1000000)
Motor = []

# We are using 2 motors with IDs 0 and 1
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=Communication1))
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=1, communication=Communication1))

timeout_setting = 0.00005

MAX_JOY_VAL = math.pow(2, 15)
DEADBAND_THRESHOLD = 0.1

# Read xbox controller and output left joystick x and y positions
def read_left_joystick():
    left_joystick_x = 0
    left_joystick_y = 0
    
    def monitor_left_joystick():
        nonlocal left_joystick_x, left_joystick_y
        while True:
            events = get_gamepad()
            for event in events:
                if event.code == 'ABS_Y':
                    left_joystick_y = event.state / MAX_JOY_VAL  # normalize between -1 and 1
                elif event.code == 'ABS_X':
                    left_joystick_x = event.state / MAX_JOY_VAL  # normalize between -1 and 1

                  # Apply deadband
                if abs(left_joystick_x) < DEADBAND_THRESHOLD:
                    left_joystick_x = 0
                if abs(left_joystick_y) < DEADBAND_THRESHOLD:
                    left_joystick_y = 0

    monitor_thread = threading.Thread(target=monitor_left_joystick)
    monitor_thread.daemon = True
    monitor_thread.start()

    while True:
        yield left_joystick_x, left_joystick_y

# Robot control 
def control_robot():
    for x, y in read_left_joystick():
        # Assuming the robot has two wheels and speed can be controlled independently
        left_wheel_speed = y + x
        right_wheel_speed = y - x
        
        # Limit the speed between -1 and 1
        left_wheel_speed = max(min(left_wheel_speed, 1), -1)
        right_wheel_speed = max(min(right_wheel_speed, 1), -1)
        
        # Use the calculated speeds to control the robot's wheels        
        print("Left Wheel Speed:", left_wheel_speed)
        print("Right Wheel Speed:", right_wheel_speed)

        # Send data to all motors
        Motor[0].Send_data_pack_1(None,int(left_wheel_speed * 1000000),0)
        Motor[1].Send_data_pack_1(None,int(right_wheel_speed * -1000000),0)

        for i in range(1, 4):  # Loop 9-1=8 to check for received data
            message, UnpackedMessageID = Communication1.receive_can_messages(timeout=timeout_setting)
            print(f"unpack{i} is: {UnpackedMessageID}")

            # Check if UnpackedMessageID is not None 
            if UnpackedMessageID is not None:
                
                Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].UnpackData(message,UnpackedMessageID)
                print(f"Motor {UnpackedMessageID[0]}, speed is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].speed}")

        time.sleep(0.05)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    control_robot()

```

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/guides/quadruped/ -->

# Quadruped robot guide

## Intro
In this guide we will show you how you can control a leg of any quadruped robot using Spectral micro BLDC drivers. <br />If you can control one of them you can control all the rest!<br />

**After you finish this guide you will be able to do something like this: [Link](https://youtu.be/g9rHJr9-tok) **<br />

!!! tip "Python API and toolbox"
    This guide leverages [Spectral BLDC python API](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-Python/tree/main) and [Source robotics toolbox](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Source-Robotics-Toolbox)

![drawing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/LEG_wiring.webp)

!!! note "Building the LEG"
    In this guide we only recommend you the hardware you can use to build the robot you designed. We do not offer already made designs you can build!

This guide will cover:

* How to define the robot leg kinematic chain
* How to execute simple trajectories with the leg

What you will need:

* 2 x spectral micro BLDC 
* Wires to connect everything up: [CAN wires](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-can-cable), [Power wires](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-power-cable)
* 2 x BLDC motors
* 1 x [CAN adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/canvas-usb-to-can-adapter)
* 1 x 24V power supply
* A Laptop or raspberry pi

![drawing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/leg_setup.webp)

The setup will be the same for any kind of quadruped leg. You will need to follow the diagram above to wire everything up.

* First you need to calibrate your Spectral BLDC drivers with the motors you are using. 
* After that change the CAN ids of one of the drivers to CAN 1. You can do it by using UART commands: #CANID 1 and after that #Save
* Now connect CAN adapters CAN bus to one of the drivers and then from that driver connect to the second driver. Make sure that last driver in chain has its CAN termination resistor in "ON" state
* Connect the power to both drivers. (Use daisy chain)

## Leg kinematics

![drawing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/robot_leg_dh_table.webp)

First you will need to assign coordinate frames to your leg model.
We already did it but if you want to learn more on how and why check this [Link](https://automaticaddison.com/how-to-assign-denavit-hartenberg-frames-to-robotic-arms/)<br />

Now we will need to find DH (Denavit-Hartenberg) table values. You can learn more on how and why we did it [Here!](https://automaticaddison.com/how-to-find-denavit-hartenberg-parameter-tables/)

value l1 is 0.112 meters and value l2 is 0.1 meters. The frame 2 is the end / foot of our leg.

## Testing / Calibrating the leg

Before running the main code lets check if the comms are working and get initial position values of our robot leg. This code will try to get data from the 2 motors of our robot leg. We are most interested in position data of those 2 motors. Position the leg like shown in this image. Run the leg_calib code and write down position values of each motor. 

![drawing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/leg_terminal.webp)

``` py title="leg_calib.py"

import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
import time

Communication1 = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM6', bitrate=1000000)
Motor = []

Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=Communication1))
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=1, communication=Communication1)) 

timeout_setting = 0.00005

while True:

    Motor[0].Send_Respond_Encoder_data()
    Motor[1].Send_Respond_Encoder_data()

    for i in range(1, 7):  # Loop 9-1=8 to check for received data
        message, UnpackedMessageID = Communication1.receive_can_messages(timeout=timeout_setting)
        print(f"unpack {i} is: {UnpackedMessageID}")

        # Check if UnpackedMessageID is not None 
        if UnpackedMessageID is not None:
            #print(Motor)
            # Update received id index; meaning that we received response from that CAN ID
            Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].UnpackData(message,UnpackedMessageID)
            print(f"Motor {UnpackedMessageID [0]}, speed is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].speed}, current is {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].current },pos is {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position}")
            """

            print(f"Encoder error is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].encoder_error}")
            print(f"Vbus error is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].vbus_error}")
            print(f"Driver error is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].driver_error}")
            print(f"Velocity error is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].velocity_error}")
            print(f"Current error is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].current_error}")
            print(f"Estop error is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].estop_error}")

            print(f"Activated is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].activated}")
            """

    time.sleep(0.5)
``` 

## Follow a specific trajectory

Joint level control involves directly controlling the angles or positions of the robot's individual joints. Each joint is treated as an independent actuator, and the control system sends commands to each joint to achieve the desired angles. 

For this example we will not use joint level control but a different method called Task/Cartesian Level Control.<br />
 Task or cartesian level control focuses on controlling the position and orientation of the robot's end-effector in a Cartesian coordinate system (X, Y, Z coordinates and orientations). In our robot leg case we don't have Z axes (or orientation) and our end-effector is foot (end of our robot leg).

In this example we will follow a circle trajectory i X,Y plane.
We defined that trajectory with our function generate_circle_coords and with parameters: 

* center - Tuple representing the center coordinates (x, y) in meters
* radius - Radius of the circle in meters
* speed - Speed of the end-effector in meters per second
* time_var - Elapsed time in seconds

![drawing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/circ_2.webp)

How precise you follow the trajectory depends on the speed you set. With low speeds you can track the circle perfectly. With larger speeds the system can't keep up and overshoots. This is due multiple reaseons like:

* Inertia and Momentum: At higher speeds, the inertia and momentum of the robot leg increase, making it harder to change directions quickly and accurately.
* Centrifugal and Coriolis Forces
* Trajectory Planning and Execution - at higher speeds our trajectory has less points to create a full circle. This is due a fixed rate we send data to our motors eg. every 20ms. 
* Feedforward Control: Lack of proper feedforward control can lead to errors in trajectory tracking, as the controller might not anticipate the required accelerations and decelerations.

You can see that from the example with speed set to 1 and 3.

## Example code

This code will make your robot leg draw the above circles. It might look complicated but it is not. Once you understand how this example works you can use it as a base for building more complicated projects. 

``` py title="2DOF_leg_demo.py"
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
import SourceRoboticsToolbox as SourceRoboticsToolbox
import time
import numpy as np
# We are using v1.1.0
from roboticstoolbox import DHRobot, RevoluteDH, ERobot, ELink, ETS
from math import pi, sin, cos
from spatialmath import *
from oclock import Timer, loop, interactiveloop
import math
from typing import Union, Any, List, Optional, cast
INTERVAL_S = 0.02

Needed_joint_pos = np.array([14000,2430]) # These are the positions we got from calib code
Joint_reduction_ratio = [1, 0.90476190] # Reduction ratio we have on our joints

# Setup your CAN coms. Change the channel to match your CAN adapter
Communication1 = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM6', bitrate=1000000)

# Define our motors
Motor: list[Union[Spectral.SpectralCAN,Spectral.SpectralCAN]] = []
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=Communication1))
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=1, communication=Communication1))

# Define the joints
Joint: list[Union[SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint,SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint]] = []
Joint.append(SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint(encoder_resolution = 14, master_position=Needed_joint_pos[0], gear_ratio = Joint_reduction_ratio[0], offset = -np.pi/2, dir = 0))
Joint.append(SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint(encoder_resolution = 14, master_position=Needed_joint_pos[1], gear_ratio = Joint_reduction_ratio[1], offset = 0, dir = 0))

timeout_setting = 0.001

initial = 0
initial_setup = [0,0]

testing = 5

# Initialize position values
position_values =  np.array([0.0,0.0])
Motor_values = np.array([0,0])
received_ids = [0,0]

# robot length values (metres)
l = [0.112, 0.1]

alpha_DH = [0,0]

# Create robot model using DH params
L1 = RevoluteDH(a=l[0],d = 0,alpha=alpha_DH[0])
L2 = RevoluteDH(a=l[1],d = 0,alpha=alpha_DH[1])
robot = DHRobot([L1,L2], name="Two link")

prev_pos = np.array([0,0])
speed_var = np.array([0,0])

def generate_circle_coords(center, radius, speed, time):
  """
  Generates x,y coordinates for a circle at a given time, considering constant speed.

  Args:
      center: Tuple representing the center coordinates (x, y) in meters.
      radius: Radius of the circle in meters.
      speed: Speed of the end-effector in meters per second.
      time: Elapsed time in seconds.

  Returns:
      Tuple containing the x and y coordinates in meters.
  """

  # Calculate angular displacement based on speed and time
  angular_displacement = speed * time

  # Use parametric equations for a circle to generate coordinates
  x = center[0] + radius * math.cos(angular_displacement)
  y = center[1] + radius * math.sin(angular_displacement)

  return (x, y)

def save_xy_data(filename, xy_data):
  """
  Saves a list of x,y coordinates to a text file.

  Args:
      filename (str): The name of the text file to save the data to.
      xy_data (list): A list of tuples containing x and y coordinates.
  """

  with open(filename, 'a') as file:
    for x, y in xy_data:
      file.write(f"{x},{y}\n")
  
# Example usage with update loop (adjust update_interval for your needs)
center = (-0.04, -0.17)
radius = 0.03
speed = 0.8
time_var = 0

# We are using oclock module to generate stable interval defined with INTERVAL_S
timer = Timer(interval=INTERVAL_S, warnings=False, precise=True)
while timer.elapsed_time < 1100000:

    t1 = time.perf_counter()
    #Motor[0].Send_Respond_Encoder_data()
    #Motor[1].Send_Respond_Encoder_data()
    Motor[0].Send_data_pack_1(Position = Needed_joint_pos[0],Speed = speed_var[0], Current = 0)
    Motor[1].Send_data_pack_1(Position = Needed_joint_pos[1],Speed = speed_var[1], Current = 0)

    # Handles data we get from the motors
    for i in range(1, 3):  # Loop 9-1=8 to check for received data
        message, UnpackedMessageID = Communication1.receive_can_messages(timeout=timeout_setting)
        #print(f"unpack{i} is: {UnpackedMessageID}")

        # Check if UnpackedMessageID is not None 
        if UnpackedMessageID is not None:
            
            # Update received id index; meaning that we received response from that CAN ID
            received_ids[UnpackedMessageID[0]] = 1
            Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].UnpackData(message,UnpackedMessageID)
            #print(f"Motor {UnpackedMessageID[0]}, position is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position}")
            unwrapped_position_raw = Joint[UnpackedMessageID[0]].unwrap_position(Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position)
            Motor_values[UnpackedMessageID[0]] = Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position
            position_values[UnpackedMessageID[0]] =  Joint[UnpackedMessageID[0]].get_joint_position(Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position)

            if initial_setup[UnpackedMessageID[0]] == 0:
                initial_setup[UnpackedMessageID[0]] = 1
                Joint[UnpackedMessageID[0]].determine_sector(Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position)

    # Generate desired x,y coordinates with respect to time_var
    x, y = generate_circle_coords(center, radius, speed, time_var)

    # Create a matrix with those x,y coordinates
    T2 = SE3(x, y, 0)
    # Perform inverse kinematics (get joint data from x,y data)
    q1 = robot.ik_LM(T2, q0 = [-0.8,-1],mask = [1,1,0,0,0,0])
    Needed_joint_pos[0] = Joint[0].get_encoder_position(q1[0][0])
    Needed_joint_pos[1] = Joint[1].get_encoder_position(q1[0][1])  
    speed_var[0] = ((Needed_joint_pos[0] - prev_pos[0]) / INTERVAL_S)
    speed_var[1] = ((Needed_joint_pos[1] - prev_pos[1]) / INTERVAL_S)
    print(speed_var)
    prev_pos[0] = Needed_joint_pos[0]
    prev_pos[1] = Needed_joint_pos[1]
    # Process or visualize the generated coordinates (x, y)
    #print(f"Time: {time_var:.2f}s, Coordinates: ({x:.4f}, {y:.4f})")

    # Update time
    time_var += INTERVAL_S

    t2 = time.perf_counter()
    #print(f"total time is {t2-t1}")

    T = robot.fkine(position_values)
    xy = T.t
    #print(f"{xy[0]},{xy[1]}")
    xy_data = [(xy[0], xy[1])]  # Assuming xy is a single pair of coordinates
    # Save data to a txt file
    save_xy_data('my_data.txt', xy_data)
    #time.sleep(0.05)

```

## Plot data

Script that will plot the data of your leg:

``` py title="plot_leg_data.py"

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def plot_data(filename):
  """
  Plots data from a text file in the format:
  x1, y1
  x2, y2
  ...

  Args:
      filename (str): The name of the text file containing the data.
  """

  try:
    with open(filename, 'r') as file:
      data = file.readlines()

    x_data = []
    y_data = []
    for line in data:
      # Split the line based on comma (",")
      values = line.strip().split(',')

      # Check if there are exactly two values per line
      if len(values) != 2:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid line format in file '{filename}': {line}")

      try:
        x = float(values[0])
        y = float(values[1])
      except ValueError:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid data type in file '{filename}': {line}")

      x_data.append(x)
      y_data.append(y)

    # Ensure equal x and y scales
    plt.axis('equal')

    # Create the plot
    plt.plot(x_data, y_data)

    # Customize the plot (optional)
    plt.xlabel('X-Position')
    plt.ylabel('Y-Position')
    plt.title('Data Plot from ' + filename)

    plt.grid(True)
    plt.show()

  except FileNotFoundError:
    print(f"Error: File '{filename}' not found.")
  except (ValueError, TypeError) as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")

# Example usage
filename = 'C:\\Users\\xx\\Desktop\\test_code\\env\\Robot_leg\\data_2.txt'  # Replace with your actual filename
plot_data(filename)

```

# Gravity compensation

<iframe width="560" height="315" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/ax6jpcH3168?si=d5UKeyYru_Y35xdS" title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

## What is Gravity Compensation?

Gravity compensation is a fundamental concept in robotic control that helps counteract the effects of gravity on a robot's joints and links. By applying the necessary motor current to balance this torque, the robotic joint can remain stationary at any position without additional external forces.

## Why is it so important?

In robotics, a significant portion of motor power is consumed just fighting against gravity. Gravity compensation algorithms are standard in all industrial robots and collaborative robot arms because they provide: improved position accuracy and control, smoother motion planning, and more precise force control applications. The gravity compensation algorithm works as a feedforward component to the motor PID control loops, reducing their computational load and improving overall performance.

## The Approach

In this example, we use the Robotics Toolbox for Python to model a "robotic arm" with a single revolute joint. We compute the required torque using the Recursive Newton-Euler Algorithm (RNEA) and convert this torque into a motor current/torque that the motor controller will command the motor. In this blog post we will explain in short pseudo code snippets how the algorithm works on a single DOF arm.

For more info check the full guide here:  [https://source-robotics.com/blogs/blog/gravity-compensation-in-robotics](https://source-robotics.com/blogs/blog/gravity-compensation-in-robotics)

Github repos with examples are here: [Github repo](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-Python/blob/main/examples/Advanced/Gravity%20compensation/BOM.md), [Github repo2](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-Python/tree/main/examples/Advanced/Gravity%20compensation)


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/guides/bilateral-teleoperation/ -->

# Bilateral teleoperation guide

## What is bilateral teleoperation?
Bilateral teleoperation is a concept that Involves two-way communication where both the operator and the remote device send and receive feedback. The operator controls the device remotely and receives sensory feedback (such as force) from the device to adjust their actions.

The two grippers are virtually coupled to each other, allowing either to act as the master (the haptic interface) or the slave (the manipulator) in the system. We are not using a force sensor at the grippers but are relying on proprioception.

![drawing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/bil_tel.webp)

Watch these example videos to get a "feel" of the concept:

- [Gripper bilateral](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8jfgFuEFNdI) 
- [2DOF arm bilateral](https://twitter.com/SourceRobotics/status/1812872129148342691)

!!! note "What is this used for?"
    These kind of setup is perfect for: Teleoperation, Imitation learning, Virtual Environments...

## The algorithm
The magic of this setup is done with these 2 simple formulas.

 We got them from amazing Ben Katz paper, creator of mini cheetah quad: [Link to the paper](https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/118671?show=full)

 𝜏1,𝑖 = 𝐾𝑝(𝜃2,𝑖 − 𝜃1, 𝑖) + 𝐾𝑑( ˙𝜃2,𝑖 − ˙𝜃1,𝑖) − 𝐾( ˙𝜃1,𝑖)

 𝜏2,𝑖 = 𝐾𝑝(𝜃1,𝑖 − 𝜃2, 𝑖) + 𝐾𝑑( ˙𝜃1,𝑖 − ˙𝜃2,𝑖) − 𝐾( ˙𝜃2,𝑖)

!!! tip "Learn more!"
    You can read more on how it works in our [blog post!](https://source-robotics.com/blogs/blog/force-sensitive-grippers-for-teleoperation-and-imitation-learning)

## What you will need

We recommend these items to create a simple test jig:

* 2 x spectral micro BLDC - used for 2 wheels 
* Wires to connect everything up: [CAN wires](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-can-cable), [Power wires](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-power-cable)
* 2 x BLDC motors or SSG48 grippers
* 1 x [CAN adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/canvas-usb-to-can-adapter)
* 1 x 24V power supply
* A Laptop or raspberry pi
* [UART adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/usb-to-serial-adapter)

## Setup

Here we are showing you the setup for any 2 motors, for example we are using 2 x [ssg48 grippers](https://source-robotics.com/products/compliant-gripper) that are connected in exactly the same setup.

![drawing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/assets/leg_setup.webp)

You will need to follow the diagram above to wire everything up.

* First you need to calibrate your Spectral BLDC drivers with the motors you are using. 
* After that change the CAN ids of one of the drivers to CAN 1. You can do it by using UART commands: #CANID 1 and after that #Save
* Now connect CAN adapters CAN bus to one of the drivers and then from that driver connect to the second driver. Make sure that last driver in chain has its CAN termination resistor in "ON" state
* Connect the power to both drivers. You can daisy chain it or use 2 separate wires.

## The code

This code will run on your PC and it will communicate with the drivers from the CAN adapter.

!!! danger "Advanced example"
    More advanced code that allows communication over UDP can be found here: [Link](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-Python/tree/main/examples/Advanced/SSG48%20gripper%20bilateral%20teleop) 

``` py title="Spectral_mobile_robot_xbox.py"
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
import SourceRoboticsToolbox as SourceRoboticsToolbox
import time
import numpy as np
from math import pi, sin, cos
from spatialmath import *
from typing import Union, Any, List, Optional, cast

Needed_joint_pos = np.array([100,100]) # If using gripper you will need to adjust this
Joint_reduction_ratio = [1, 1] # Reduction ratio we have on our joints

Communication1 = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM123', bitrate=1000000)

Motor: list[Union[Spectral.SpectralCAN,Spectral.SpectralCAN]] = []
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=Communication1))
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=1, communication=Communication1))

Joint: list[Union[SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint,SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint]] = []
Joint.append(SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint(encoder_resolution = 14, master_position=Needed_joint_pos[0], gear_ratio = Joint_reduction_ratio[0], offset = 0, dir = 0))
Joint.append(SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint(encoder_resolution = 14, master_position=Needed_joint_pos[1], gear_ratio = Joint_reduction_ratio[1], offset = 0, dir = 0))

timeout_setting = 0.001

initial = 0
initial_setup = [0,0]

# Initialize position values
position_values =  np.array([0.0,0.0])
Motor_values = np.array([0,0])

speed_values = np.array([0,0])

position_send = np.array([0,0])
speed_send = np.array([0,0])
T0 = 0
T1 = 0

received_ids = [0,0] 
Kp = 650
Kd = 0.00550 #  0.0060
Kk = 0.0003 #0.0003

while(1):
    t1 = time.perf_counter()
    Motor[0].Send_data_pack_1(Position = None,Speed = None, Current = int(T0))
    Motor[1].Send_data_pack_1(Position = None,Speed = None, Current = int(T1))

    for i in range(1, 3):  # Loop 9-1=8 to check for received data
        message, UnpackedMessageID = Communication1.receive_can_messages(timeout=timeout_setting)
        #print(f"unpack{i} is: {UnpackedMessageID}")

        # Check if UnpackedMessageID is not None 
        if UnpackedMessageID is not None:
            
            # Update received id index; meaning that we received response from that CAN ID
            received_ids[UnpackedMessageID[0]] = 1
            Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].UnpackData(message,UnpackedMessageID)
            #print(f"Motor {UnpackedMessageID[0]}, position is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position}")
            unwrapped_position_raw = Joint[UnpackedMessageID[0]].unwrap_position(Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position)
            Motor_values[UnpackedMessageID[0]] = Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position
            position_values[UnpackedMessageID[0]] =  Joint[UnpackedMessageID[0]].get_joint_position(Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position)

            if initial_setup[UnpackedMessageID[0]] == 0:
                initial_setup[UnpackedMessageID[0]] = 1
                Joint[UnpackedMessageID[0]].determine_sector(Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position)

    # The magic
    T0 = Kp*( position_values[1] -  position_values[0]) + Kd*(Motor[1].speed - Motor[0].speed) - Kk*(Motor[0].speed)
    T1 = Kp*( position_values[0] -  position_values[1]) + Kd*(Motor[0].speed - Motor[1].speed) - Kk*(Motor[1].speed)
    # There are no delays here, we send as fast as possible!

```

# SimpleFOC guide

!!! tip "Tested with Simple FOC@^2.3.2 release"

**Main firmware that runs on Spectral micro is [Spectral firmware](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-Micro-BLDC-controller).**<br />

SimpleFOC is alternative to Spectral Firmware. <br />
The library is intended both for:

* Beginners searching for a simple and user-friendly way to learn how to control BLDC and Stepper motors
* Advanced users ready to dig deeper into the FOC algorithm and optimize the code for their particular application/hardware.

**More info about simple FOC:**

* [Forum](https://community.simplefoc.com/)
* [DOCS](https://docs.simplefoc.com/)
* [Discord](https://discord.com/invite/kWBwuzY32n)
!!! note "SimpleFOC forum and discord is best place to look for help when developing with SimpleFOC library"

## How to install

Follow this [guide](https://docs.simplefoc.com/installation)

Your platformio.ini should look like this:

``` C++ title="main.cpp"
[env:genericSTM32F103CB]
platform = ststm32
board = genericSTM32F103CB
framework = arduino
upload_protocol = stlink
build_flags = 
debug_tool = stlink
monitor_speed = 115200
lib_deps = 
	askuric/Simple FOC@^2.3.2
lib_archive = false
```

## SimpleFOC guides
If you want to develop more advanced applications with SimpleFOC you can follow these tutorials:

* [Getting started](https://docs.simplefoc.com/example_from_scratch)
* [Writing the code](https://docs.simplefoc.com/code)
* [SimpleFOC Driver and Support Library](https://github.com/simplefoc/Arduino-FOC-drivers/tree/master)

## Basic example

This example will spin the motor in open loop and enable serial monitor.<br />
Use this code as a base for more advanced code you will develop with SimpleFOC.<br />
In the github folder we also offer full FOC example!

``` C++ title="main.cpp"
#include "Arduino.h"
#include "SimpleFOC.h"

// Driver PWM pins
#define PWM_CH1 PA_2
#define PWM_CH2 PA_1 
#define PWM_CH3 PA_0 

// Encoder pins
#define MOSI PB_5
#define MISO PB_4
#define CLK PB_3
#define CSN PA_15

#define SENSE1 PA_4 // Inline current sense
#define SENSE2  PA_3 // Inline current sense

#define TX_COM PB_6
#define RX_COM PB_7

// Current sense resistors
#define SENSE_RESISTOR 0.025f
#define CURRENT_AMP_GAIN 20

// Serial pins
#define Serial Serialx
HardwareSerial Serialx(RX_COM, TX_COM); // PA3, PA2 RX,TX

// BLDC motor & driver instance
// BLDCMotor motor = BLDCMotor(pole pair number, phase resistance (optional) );
BLDCMotor motor = BLDCMotor(11);
//  BLDCDriver3PWM( pin_pwmA, pin_pwmB, pin_pwmC )
BLDCDriver3PWM driver = BLDCDriver3PWM(PWM_CH1, PWM_CH2, PWM_CH3);

//target variable
float target_velocity = 0.1;

void Init_pins();

void setup() {  

  // Init driver enable pins and LED
  Init_pins();

  // pwm frequency to be used [Hz]
  driver.pwm_frequency = 20000;
  // power supply voltage [V]
  driver.voltage_power_supply = 24;
  // Max DC voltage allowed - default voltage_power_supply
  driver.voltage_limit = 5;
  // driver init
  driver.init();
    // link the motor and the driver
  motor.linkDriver(&driver);
  motor.controller = MotionControlType::velocity_openloop;

  // init motor hardware
  motor.init();
    // use monitoring with the BLDCMotor
  Serial.begin(115200);
  Serial.println("Motor ready!");
  _delay(1000);
  // monitoring port
  motor.useMonitoring(Serial);

}

void loop() {
  // open loop velocity movement
  // using motor.voltage_limit and motor.velocity_limit
  motor.move(target_velocity);
  // monitoring function outputting motor variables to the serial terminal 
  motor.monitor();

}

void Init_pins(){
  pinMode(PA_9, OUTPUT);
	pinMode(PA_8, OUTPUT);
	pinMode(PA_10, OUTPUT);
	pinMode(PB_15, OUTPUT);
	pinMode(PB_14, OUTPUT);
	pinMode(PB_13, OUTPUT);

  digitalWrite(PA_9,HIGH);
  digitalWrite(PA_8,HIGH);
  digitalWrite(PA_10,HIGH);
  digitalWrite(PB_14, HIGH);
  digitalWrite(PB_15, HIGH);
  digitalWrite(PB_13, HIGH);
}
```

# Getting help

- **Questions and discussion**: the [Source Robotics Discord](https://discord.gg/prjUvjmGpZ).
- **A problem with the driver or the firmware**: an issue in the
  [firmware repository](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-Micro-BLDC-controller/issues); see
  [Report a problem](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/support/report-a-problem/) for what to include.
- **A mistake on a page of this site**: every page ends with a link to edit it and one to report it; see
  [Contributing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/support/contributing/).
- **Orders and hardware**: [source-robotics.com](https://source-robotics.com/).

Before you ask, [Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/08-troubleshooting/) goes through the common symptoms, and `#Info` tells
most of what anyone will ask you for.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/support/report-a-problem/ -->

# Report a problem

Open an issue in the [firmware repository](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-Micro-BLDC-controller/issues)
for the driver and its firmware, or in [Spectral-BLDC-Python](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-Python/issues)
for the Python library. Include:

1. **The output of `#Info`**, copied from the terminal. It carries the hardware and firmware version, the motor
   parameters, the calibration state and the errors.
2. **The motor**: type, and the resistance, inductance and pole pairs calibration found (`#Info` prints them).
3. **The supply**: voltage, and whether it has a current limit.
4. **What you did and what happened**: the commands, in order, and the driver's answers; the calibration log if it
   is about calibration.
5. **How it is wired**: a photo of the board on the motor and of the cables helps more than a description.

For a problem with this documentation, the *Report it* link at the end of the page opens an issue in the
documentation repository with the page already named.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/107/support/contributing/ -->

# Contributing

This documentation lives in [Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-docs](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-docs). A
small fix can be made from the browser: the *Edit it on GitHub* link at the end of every page opens the page's
source, and GitHub turns your change into a pull request. For anything larger, open an issue first.

## How the site is built

- The pages are Markdown, built with MkDocs and the Material theme; the repository's `README.md` says how to
  preview it locally.
- The site describes one firmware release, named in `versions.yml`. The command IDs, frame lengths, the UART
  command list and the defaults in the Reference are read from the firmware's source at that release's tag by
  `tools/sync_firmware.py`; do not edit those facts in the pages. The descriptions of the commands are in
  `docs/includes/can_commands.yml` and `uart_commands.yml`.
- Every push runs a strict build (a broken link fails it) and the tool tests. A push to `main` publishes the
  site under its firmware version with [mike](https://github.com/jimporter/mike).

## House rules

- Facts come from the firmware. When a page and the firmware disagree, the firmware is right; fix the page, or
  report the firmware.
- Spell commands exactly as the firmware does, even where the spelling looks wrong.
- Write for someone who has the driver in front of them and wants to do one thing: say what to do, in order, then
  why.
- Three kinds of boxes: a note, a notice (damage) and a danger (injury). Use them for those, not for emphasis.
- Images: under 2400 px on the long side, with a caption that says what the reader should see.
